inline.s: On the day the World-Honored One attained the Way, Ananda was born. By the time he left home, the Buddha had already taught the Dharma for twenty years; and so Ananda asked the Buddha to set forth again all that had been spoken during those first twenty years, and what he had missed was supplied. Ananda moreover attained the samadhi of Dharma-nature, the samadhi of awakened freedom, and could, within concentration, comprehend every Dharma. That is why the compilation of the Dharma-store was necessarily entrusted to Ananda; and the Buddha himself had given his consent. Thus the Lotus Sutra says: “I and Ananda, at the time of the Buddha King of Emptiness, brought forth the aspiration together. I delighted in diligence, and so attained Buddhahood; Ananda took constant delight in much hearing, and so upholds the treasury of my Dharma.” This is that very matter. At the time of the compilation, when Ananda ascended the seat, the light of his body was like the Buddha's. The assembly wondered whether the World-Honored One had risen again to teach the Dharma, or whether a Buddha from another region had come, or whether Ananda himself had become a Buddha. The moment Ananda opened his mouth and said, “Thus have I heard,” and so on, those three doubts were cut off at once. The World-Honored One had surely foreseen that such doubts would arise, and so he had every sutra begin with the words “Thus have I heard” and the rest.

Concerning the compilation itself, the sutras, the vinaya, and the treatises offer various accounts. Some say that the whole of the Small Vehicle Tripitaka was compiled by Ananda. Some say that Upali compiled the vinaya, and Ananda only the sutras and treatises. Some say that the treatises were compiled by Mahakashyapa himself; others, that the treatises were recited out by Purna. This is called the Five Hundred Council, also the First Council. It took place in the year of the World-Honored One's parinirvana, at the Vaibhara Cave outside the city of Rajagriha. King Ajatashatru was its outer protector, and the Venerable Mahakashyapa its chief. Some say there were five hundred in the assembly, some a thousand, some eighty-four thousand. It is also called the Sthavira Council, because Mahakashyapa was the elder among all the monks. The compilation began on the fifteenth day after the start of that year's rains-retreat. Some say it was finished within the three months of the rains-retreat; some say it was finished only after four months. Some say that in the twelfth month of that year the king died, Mahakashyapa also entered Wolf-Trace Mountain, and the great assembly dispersed. At that time several hundred or several thousand of the learners and adepts who had been unable to join the council, wishing to repay the Buddha's kindness, went twenty li northwest of the cave and separately compiled the sutras, the vinaya, the treatises, the miscellaneous collection, and the collection of spells, making five stores. Because both ordinary and holy beings gathered there, it is called the Mahasanghika Council. (These were all disciples of the Buddha, not the Mahasanghika of a hundred years after the Buddha's parinirvana.) The arhat Vasupashin was its chief, and King Ajatashatru was again the great donor, making all manner of offerings. This is seen in the Sutra of the Dharma Treasury, the Records of the Western Regions, and other books. After that there were three further councils. One took place about a hundred years after the Buddha's parinirvana, when the elder Yashas (also written Yashodhara, also written Shunaka) was chief and seven hundred holy ones assembled. The elder Revata questioned Sabhakami, and by their questions and answers the dispute was settled, devoted wholly to purifying the vinaya and clearing away what was contrary to Dharma. This is called the Second Council. Another took place two hundred and thirty-five years after the Buddha's parinirvana, in the time of King Ashoka, when Maudgalyayana Tishya was chief; sixty thousand gathered, and a thousand were chosen out of them. Tishya composed a treatise to refute the erroneous doctrines of the outsiders. This is the Third Council. The last took place about four or five hundred years later, in the time of King Kanishka, when five hundred arhats and five hundred bodhisattvas assembled, with Katyayaniputra as chief; the bodhisattva Ashvaghosha composed a treatise, and after twelve years the Vibhasha Treatise was completed, a million verses, to explain the sutras. (What has been translated out is a part of it.) Some say that the bodhisattva Vasumitra was chief and composed treatises on the three stores, a hundred thousand verses each. This is the Fourth Council. Some hold that compilations already existed in the Buddha's lifetime, as when Maudgalyayana composed the Treatise on the Feet of the Dharma Treasury. But these were only partial compositions. As for summoning the assembly and undertaking a compilation on a great scale, this truly began with Mahakashyapa, Ananda, and the host of holy ones.

As for the Mahayana compilation, there are roughly two accounts. One says that seven days after the Buddha's parinirvana, Mahakashyapa told the five hundred arhats to sound the mallet and gather all the arhats of the ten directions, and eighty-eight thousand assembled. Between the twin sala trees he had Ananda ascend the seat, and the three stores of bodhisattvas, hearers, and precepts were compiled in portions. The bodhisattva store had eight parts: the Womb Transformation store first, the Intermediate Existence store second, the Mahayana Vaipulya third, the Precepts store fourth, the Ten Dwellings Bodhisattva store fifth, the Miscellaneous store sixth, the Vajra store seventh, and the Buddha store eighth. This is seen in the Sutra of the Bodhisattva's Womb. The other says that Manjushri and Maitreya and the other great bodhisattvas brought Ananda to Iron Ring Mountain and there compiled the three stores of the Mahayana; this is seen in the Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom.

As for the esoteric division, there are likewise two accounts. Some say that Ananda compiled it all. Some say that the bodhisattva Vajrapani was the chief and Ananda his companion. The latter account is probably based on the Sutra of the Six Paramitas. In that sutra the Buddha gathers all Dharmas into five divisions and tells the bodhisattva Maitreya: “After my parinirvana, let Ananda receive and uphold the sutra store of what I have spoken (that is, the store of sutras); let Upali receive and uphold the vinaya store of what I have spoken (that is, the store of precepts); let Katyayana receive and uphold the abhidharma of what I have spoken (that is, the Dharma-analysis, which is the treatise store); let Manjushri receive and uphold the great-vehicle prajnaparamita of what I have spoken; and let the bodhisattva Vajrapani receive and uphold the profoundly subtle dharani-gateways of all Dharmas that I have spoken.” This is that very matter.

The manifestation of Dharma. To manifest Dharma means to dissolve everything back into one's own nature. In hearing a sutra and listening to the Dharma, what matters is to melt the words of the sutra and bring each point home to one's own nature for realization; only then is there any benefit. The passage before us is in origin a matter of circumstance and appearance, yet it can still be dissolved back into one's own nature. From this the later passages of the sutra may be understood by analogy. Extending the point: if one can receive every circumstance in this way, the benefit is inexhaustible. Take note, take note.

“Thus” (ru) means suchness, unmoving, and points to the essence of the nature that each person inherently possesses. “Is” (shi) means that it is exactly so right now. Though this nature is exactly so right now for every ordinary being, yet arising and ceasing do not halt for an instant, and it is not suchness. Why? Only because the clinging to a self obstructs it. Therefore one must break through the clinging to a small self and return to the great self. The great self is what is called the one Dharma-realm: mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are three with no difference, and it is the self of permanence, bliss, true self, and purity. The word “self” here should be understood in this way. “Heard” (wen) means to turn the hearing around and hear one's own nature. If one would return home, one must turn the hearing inward; one cannot go chasing outward, turning from enlightenment and joining with dust. “At one time” (yi shi) means that the ten periods and ancient and modern times do not depart from the present thought; it also means that the mind of the three periods is unobtainable. This is how it should be understood.

The word “I” in the passage above is meant to bring one to realize the one Dharma-realm, so that the obstruction of space is removed. The word “at one time” here is meant to bring one to realize the absence of the three periods, so that the obstruction of time is likewise removed. The original nature is just so, just so; one should turn the hearing around in this very way. Ordinary beings have long since forgotten their original face. Now, wishing to turn the light back, they must have a skillful means. Among the six faculties, none is so perfect and penetrating as the ear. It is as said: strike a drum in ten directions, and the ten directions hear it at once. In the nature itself there is fundamentally no obstruction, and this is comparatively easy to realize. Therefore one is led to enter by way of the ear, because the ear faculty is complete in its twelve hundred virtues. (Twelve hundred is only a figure for its perfection and non-obstruction. For the guiding principles of the ten directions are only the four cardinal directions. (The four corners and above and below are all unfolded from east, south, west, and north, and so these four are the guides for the remaining six; this is spoken horizontally. The three periods are spoken vertically. Horizontal and vertical interwoven make twelve. To express their inexhaustibleness, it is said to be twelve hundred.) Multiplied by the three periods, it makes twelve; a hundredfold of that makes twelve hundred.)

“Buddha” means the innate Buddha of one's own nature. Doubly negating and doubly illuminating, the Middle Way perfect and interfused: the nature itself is thus, and this is the Shravasti of one's own nature. Vanquishing the maras of the five aggregates and continuing and prospering the Buddha-seed: this is the Prince Jeta of one's own nature. Adorning merit and wisdom, a grove of virtue: this is what is meant by “grove.” The son who abandoned his father and fled now returns to his home, inherits his father's estate, and gains the pearl in his coat without labor: this is the Anathapindada Garden of one's own nature. “Great” means great compassion and great vows. “Monk” means far from dust and free of defilement. “Assembly” means principle and phenomena in harmony. “Twelve hundred” means the perfect virtue of the ear's turning back to hear. “Fifty-five persons” means the fifty-five stages: the ten faiths, the ten dwellings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the four preparatory practices, the ten grounds, and equal enlightenment. The meaning is that the unmoving nature of suchness is exactly so right now. If one can truly be unobstructed horizontally and vertically, and thus turn the hearing around, then the innate Buddha of one's own nature is present just so. And with the fifty-five stages of bodhisattva-mahasattvas, whose great compassion and great vows, freedom from dust and defilement, harmony of principle and phenomena, and perfect virtue of turning back to hear, one becomes their companion. Then the Dharma assembly at Vulture Peak is still visibly gathered and has not dispersed. One may say that one personally heard the wondrous Dharma at Vulture Peak; and one may equally say that Vulture Peak is here in this very inch of mind. Why so? Because the innate Buddha of one's own nature and Shakyamuni Buddha have already sealed mind with mind and illumined each other with light. One has thus already seen that the circumstances of the preface of certifying faith are no-appearance, and so has seen the Tathagata. Therefore, good friends, this “thus” is not “thus” only when facing the sutra text and not “thus” when not facing it; nor is it “thus” only upon this seat of lecturing and listening and not “thus” when one leaves the seat; nor again is it “thus” only in the Dharma assembly and not “thus” outside it. One should, in every time, every matter, and every circumstance, see all appearances as no-appearance. Then movement and stillness are one suchness, and there is nowhere that is not so. Take care, take care.
(C) Next, the section of setting forth.

[At that time the World-Honored One, at the hour for the meal, put on his robe, took up his bowl, and entered the great city of Shravasti to beg for food. In that city, having begged in order from house to house, he returned to his original place. When the meal was finished, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, spread his seat, and sat down.]

For those who leave home the Buddha instituted the three robes. One is called antarvasa, rendered here as “five-strip.” (The cloth is cut into squares, sewn and joined like a field, whence it is called the field-of-merit robe. In the five-strip robe the squares are large; in the nine-strip robe the squares become gradually smaller.) It is also called the vestment worn against the body, worn when working and when sitting or lying down. One is called uttarasanga, rendered here as “seven-strip.” When lecturing on the sutras and teaching the Dharma, it is worn over the five-strip robe, and so it is also called the upper robe. (The five-strip is also called the lower grade, the seven-strip the middle grade, and the nine-strip the upper grade.) If one is among a dense crowd of people, or enters a great metropolis, or a royal palace, then one wears the nine-strip robe, in Sanskrit samghati, also called the great robe. Now, since he was about to enter the city to beg, he purposely put on the great robe. The three robes are collectively called kashaya. Kashaya means “mixed.” It is not only that the colors blue, yellow, red, black, and purple make it mixed. (This follows the Brahma Net Sutra. Other books speak only of blue, black, and red, or only of red, or say that on a red robe dots of blue and black and the like are added.) It is because the true or primary red is not used, but is mixed with blue, or with yellow, or with black, or with purple. Not only is the red not primary red; the blue, yellow, black, and purple are likewise not primary blue, primary yellow, primary black, or primary purple. This is what is meant by “mixed.” (This way of putting it gathers many accounts and harmonizes them, so that one knows it to be so; in ancient times no one stated it so plainly.) Therefore red leaning toward blue becomes the color of black mud, and so it is called “wearing black.” Red mixed with yellow is called the color of lotus-tree bark. The purple color is likewise red mixed with black; all are non-primary colors. Hence they are also called improper colors, spoiled colors, dyed colors. The reason for this is that it distinguishes them from householders and also shows the meaning of not abiding in color. (The Ekottara Agama says: “Dye it into a kashaya robe; its taste is the kashaya taste.” Therefore to gloss kashaya as “mixed” is most fitting.) A color such as this is dim and lusterless, and this too is the meaning of not displaying oneself. Putting on the robe, taking up the bowl, begging for food, and the rest were all instituted by the precepts. That the World-Honored One did so was himself setting the example and teaching people to uphold the precepts. The bowl and the rest are as usually explained.

Begging for food has many meanings. Briefly: it subdues pride; it does not crave flavors (this household gives sweet food, another may give salty, whence it is called the kashaya taste); it concentrates the mind on cultivating the Way (the foregoing is spoken from the side of the one who has left home); and it causes those who see one to give rise to a mind of shame. One who leaves home does so fundamentally to save living beings. To save living beings, one must first cut off delusion. To cut off delusion, one must practice austerities. Let ordinary people see this and give rise to shame, saying: “For the sake of saving living beings he afflicts himself like this; are we then to be so greedy for food and comfort?” Then perhaps the mind of the Way grows and worldly thoughts diminish. So the benefit of begging to living beings is great; it is not merely causing people to give and plant fields of merit. Therefore begging is itself the cultivation of the greatest merit by one who has left home. The ancient worthies, fearing that faith was not abundant and that they would surely meet with slander, had no choice but to set aside fields and plant them themselves; this already went against the Buddha's institution, and was already most painful to them. How can it be, as people today say, that monks should also run other businesses? Then why need one leave home at all? To destroy the Buddha-Dharma is greatly impermissible. If the Buddha-Dharma is to flourish greatly, the system of begging for food must be practiced. If one says that it cannot be practiced in the East, or cannot be practiced today, then Siam still follows the Buddha's institution to this day; how can it be seen that it cannot be practiced in the East today? It is only that those of faith must be many; then it can be practiced. To spread the seat and sit down is in order to enter concentration. According to the rule, before sitting there is still walking meditation. That it is not mentioned here shows the importance of applying effort, and that one must not steal a moment's ease.

That this great sutra is set forth by way of the ordinary affairs of daily use is most extraordinary. Therefore Subhuti opened his mouth and sighed, “How rare!” Yet the extraordinary is in truth no different from the ordinary; therefore Subhuti continued and said, “Well does he protect in thought and well does he entrust.” One may see that this passage bears on the whole sutra, its principle most profound and subtle yet intimate. If one reads it carelessly, does one not wrong it? Now I open ten layers and briefly clarify the meaning. The first four layers clarify it by way of the Dharma; the last six clarify it by way of teaching and transformation.

(1) In manifesting himself as putting on the robe and begging for food, hurrying about in the dust of toil, exactly like an ordinary man, the Buddha did not abide in the Buddha-appearance. That is, he displayed the Buddha's no-self-appearance. The whole sutra's purport lies in breaking the self. Now he displays no-self and speaks not a word; this also displays the Buddha's no-Dharma-appearance. Though he speaks not a word, he in fact teaches the Dharma of no-self. And thereby he also displays that the Buddha has no no-Dharma-appearance either. The principle of the three emptinesses is utterly and completely revealed. This is what is meant by “well does he entrust.”

(2) What has been clarified above is great wisdom. One who practices the bodhisattva path must be complete in both compassion and wisdom. Therefore, when he entered upon the detailed discourse, as soon as he opened his mouth he had them save all sentient beings whatsoever. And now, in showing himself the same as an ordinary man, this is the “companionship” among the four means of gathering. It is our World-Honored One's great compassion and great pity, not abandoning sentient beings, himself setting the example and becoming a model for the bodhisattva-mahasattvas. This is what is meant by “well does he protect in thought.” Viewed together: with great wisdom he practices great compassion, empty yet not empty; through great compassion he reveals great wisdom, existent yet not existent. Empty yet not empty is called wondrous existence. Existent yet not existent is true emptiness. Is this not at once emptiness and the provisional, at once the provisional and emptiness, the two truths contemplated as interfused, plainly the ultimate meaning of the Middle Way? Thus, amid ordinary daily use, he has already brought out the whole essential purport of the sutra — the principle revealing the three emptinesses and the contemplation fusing the two truths — and set it all before us. This is what is meant by “how rare.”

(3) When the Buddha taught other sutras, he often emitted light and shook the earth as the setting forth. This showed that all Dharmas issue from the right wisdom of prajna, that is, that every Dharma is nothing but prajna. In the earlier prajna teachings as well he had emitted light and shaken the earth, showing that the right wisdom of prajna can uproot fundamental ignorance. Now, in the ninth assembly, when he taught the Diamond Prajna, he did not do so again: this shows that he did not grasp even at the Dharma-appearance of prajna. Therefore this sutra says: “When the Buddha speaks of prajna-paramita, it is then not prajna-paramita.” One should know that only when one does not grasp even at prajna is it prajna-paramita. This is the utmost limit of not grasping at appearances.

(4) In the several decades before this sutra was taught, he displayed this day after day; and in the several decades after this sutra was taught, right up to his parinirvana, he likewise displayed this day after day. One may see that what is called “display” is only what others saw as such; the Buddha had no such thought as “I make this display for the great assembly.” For there was not a single instant when he was not in the great emptiness samadhi in which the two truths are interfused. What others saw as a display all flowed forth freely from that great emptiness samadhi. The Buddha, however, acted without affair, from the first having no room in his mind for it. This is the utmost limit of unmoving suchness. The whole sutra's thousands of words and phrases come down to this: “receive and uphold, read and recite, and expound for others.” How does one expound for others? “Not grasping at appearances, unmoving suchness.” One may know that these eight characters are the vital point of the whole sutra, and also the vital point for students who receive, uphold, and expound it. Now, in ordinary daily use, he displays precisely the vital point of the Diamond Prajna. May this not be called rare, well protected in thought, well entrusted? Above, the meaning of the section of setting forth has been clarified by way of the Dharma.

(5) All sentient beings alike possess the Buddha-nature; that is, every person inherently possesses the Dharmakaya Tathagata. Yet their Dharmakaya Tathagata is hidden and does not appear. The reason it is hidden and does not appear, and is not called Tathagata but only called Tathagata-store, is that, hurrying about for food and clothing, turning from enlightenment and joining with dust, they have long since forgotten their original state. Now he displays the Dharmakaya Tathagata as the same as an ordinary man, hurrying about in the dust of toil, for no other reason than to make every sentient being amid the dust of toil turn the light around and shine back upon the Tathagata-store that each inherently possesses.

(6) Ordinary beings of the broad earth have deep obstructions and heavy karma. If they now wish to turn the light back, they cannot do so without good guidance and diligent cultivation and permeation. Now he teaches this sutra and sets it forth by way of begging for food and the like in order to point out to sentient beings that in receiving and upholding this sutra they should regard it as their daily tea and rice, from which they cannot be parted for a single day. Permeated thus for a long time, perhaps faith will grow, and light will show through the thick shell of ignorance.

(7) Yet this sutra of the supreme vehicle is most profound and subtle. Now that one has seen, heard, received, and upheld it, if one wishes to comprehend the Tathagata's true meaning, one cannot enter the gate without possessing the proper qualifications. This sutra says: “In the last five hundred years there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit, and who can give rise to faith in these chapter-phrases, taking them as true.” Faith is the gate of entering the Way. To take them as true is to understand their true meaning. One may see that to understand their true meaning is true faith. Above he asked about giving rise to true faith. Now the answer is: they can give rise to faith, taking them as true. This plainly tells us that the ability to give rise to faith comes from taking them as true, that is, from truly understanding; and this is true faith. True faith is distinguished from the careless and slack kind of faith. And true faith comes from upholding the precepts and cultivating merit. If so, then for one who would enter this gate, are upholding the precepts and cultivating merit not important? Why is it that upholding the precepts and cultivating merit can give rise to faith and take these as true? The connection here is most refined and subtle; it will be explained in detail in the text that follows. Now the matters of putting on the robe, taking up the bowl, begging for food, and so on are all precepts instituted by the Buddha. To practice accordingly is to uphold the precepts. And begging for food causes all who see and hear to give rise to shame and to increase their thought of the Way; it is not merely causing them to practice giving and plant fields of merit — it is the cultivation of merit. That the Diamond Prajna is set forth by way of one who upholds the precepts and cultivates merit is precisely to point out to sentient beings the preliminary skillful means for giving rise to faith and entering the gate.

(8) Begging for food and so on are the upholding of precepts. To spread the seat and sit down is in order to enter concentration. From precepts comes concentration, and from concentration comes wisdom. Therefore this section, which serves as the setting forth of the Diamond Prajna, also points out to sentient beings the definite sequence of the three undefiled studies. It makes clear that upholding the precepts and cultivating merit can give rise to true faith and so enter the gate. Yet if the right wisdom of prajna is to appear before one, one cannot do so without cultivating concentration.

(9) The essence of cultivation lies in fusing principle and phenomena. In stillness one nurtures a glimpse of it; and one should further, when meeting circumstances and following conditions, diligently test and verify it. The ancients called this “forging the mind through affairs.” This is the most essential point in cultivation. The principle of not grasping at either extreme must be realized while eating and dressing, and must be accomplished amid ordinary daily use. Then perhaps one may reach the point where movement and stillness are one, and there is nowhere that is not so. This again is the subtle intent in the setting forth of prajna by way of begging for food and the like.

(10) There is something even more wondrous: this section of setting forth precisely points out the means of taking up practice for people amid the dust of toil. Since one is dragged along by former karma and has fallen into this stinking bag of skin, who can avoid hurrying about for food and clothing? To chase the branch and forget the root is assuredly wrong; but if because one cannot shake off the dust of toil one gives rise to affliction, that too is unacceptable. The Way lies in skillfully making use of one's circumstances: then what place is not a place of practice? Every morning, put on the robe and go out, each diligently attending to the duty of begging; when the task is done, return. As for social engagements and other irrelevant matters, omit whatever can be omitted. These four words, “returned to his original place,” should be eyed urgently. After returning, finish the matters of food and drink and washing and the rest that should be handled and put in order; then one should sit quietly, gather the thoughts, and contemplate the mind. These four words, “spread his seat and sat down,” should be eyed even more. People today are busy all day long, their social engagements many, and after returning they do not gather themselves in stillness. Even if they recite the Buddha's name and chant sutras without omitting their daily lessons, this mind has never once spent the least effort in quiet gathering. So although they recite, their deluded thoughts fly in confusion — what benefit is there? And as for the principles of not grasping at appearances, and of not grasping at no-appearance, that is, of not grasping at either the Dharma or the no-Dharma, they never attend to them or realize them. So after many years of cultivation they still shift the moment they meet circumstances and turn as conditions turn; their footing is not firm for an instant, and they themselves have not the least benefit. They may even grossly break the precepts and stop at nothing, thinking themselves free of Dharma-appearance, unaware that they have long since grasped at no-Dharma-appearance. They fall themselves, and drag countless good men and faithful women down with them. All this comes from never having gathered the thoughts and contemplated the mind, and never having realized and understood the essential meaning of not abiding in appearances and not grasping at either extreme; thus it comes about — is it not pitiable? Therefore in this passage the eight words “returned to his original place, spread his seat and sat down” are precisely the needle at the crown of the head and the motto at the side of the seat for us beings who hurry about in the dust of toil. That this is taken as the setting forth precisely shows that prajna is not something to be talked about emptily. One must rely on the words, give rise to contemplation, never relax for a moment, and diligently test and verify in every matter; only then may one comprehend some small part. Above, the meaning of the section of setting forth has been clarified by way of teaching and transformation. These ten meanings together serve as the setting forth. Not only are the principle and phenomena of the unsurpassed great Dharma wholly revealed; the methods of preparation and the means of entry for cultivators are all contained herein as well. How truly rare! If one does not comprehend them one by one and cultivate according to Dharma, will one not wrong not only the rare World-Honored One who protects in thought and entrusts, but also this rareSECTION of setting forth?
“At that time.” This is precisely when the speaking and the hearing were both complete and the conditions had ripened.

“World-Honored One” (shi zun) — there are separately the ten titles, and these are collectively called World-Honored One. Because he possesses the virtue of the ten titles and is honored by the world, he is called World-Honored One. Following the Great Treatise, the ten titles are: (1) Tathagata. All Dharmas are one suchness, which is “such”; not coming yet coming, which is “coming.” This expresses the virtue by way of the nature-substance. (2) Worthy of Offerings. He is worthy of the offerings of gods and humans; this expresses the virtue by way of great compassion and great vows. (3) Fully Enlightened. He knows all Dharmas as at once provisional and at once empty, none of them outside the Middle Way. When one is empty, all is empty; when one is provisional, all is provisional; when one is middle, all is middle; without partiality or leaning, still and illumining at once, this is “fully.” The principle and wisdom of the three truths are perfect and unobstructed; wisdom reaches throughout the sandy realms and penetrates to the finest dust: this is “enlightened.” This expresses the virtue by way of stillness and illumination at once. (4) Perfect in Clarity and Practice. There are two accounts. The Mahaparinirvana Sutra says: “Clarity” means having attained immeasurable good fruit (referring to anuttara-bodhi); “perfect in practice” means the feet that can walk (referring to precepts and wisdom, and concentration is included therein). That is, one attains supreme bodhi by riding on the feet of precepts and wisdom. This expresses the virtue by way of cultivating the cause and achieving the fruit. The Great Treatise says: “Clarity” means the three clarities of past lives, the divine eye, and the extinction of outflows; “practice” refers to the three karmas of body, speech, and mind. Only the Buddha is complete in the practice of the three clarities. Spoken according to this meaning, it expresses the virtue by way of spiritual powers. (5) Well Gone. It is like saying “a good departure.” It means entering nirvana without residue, the so-called “when birth and cessation have ceased, still extinction appears before one.” This expresses the virtue by way of cutting off and realizing. (6) Knower of the World. The circumstances of all sentient and insentient beings he understands without exception; this expresses the virtue by way of the wisdom attained afterward. (7) Unsurpassed One. Among all sentient beings the Buddha is unsurpassed; this expresses the virtue by way of his position. (8) Tamer of Men. Whether with gentle words or with piercing words, he can skillfully tame men and lead them into the good path. (It makes no difference whether man or woman, monk or layperson: if one wishes to be far from dust and free of defilement, one cannot do so without the spirit of a great man and a mind resolute and firm. Such a person only the Buddha can tame and drive.) This expresses the virtue by way of being the teacher of the teaching. (9) Teacher of Gods and Humans. He is the model for gods and humans. As sunlight shines everywhere, none fails to receive its benefit; this expresses the virtue by way of universal benefit. (10) Buddha. Self-enlightened, enlightening others, and complete in enlightenment — this is called Buddha. This expresses the virtue by way of the fruit of ultimate enlightenment. Other sutras and treatises sometimes combine Worthy of Offerings and Fully Enlightened into one, calling it “Worthy and Fully Enlightened”; or combine Well Gone and Knower of the World into one; or combine Unsurpassed One and Tamer of Men into one; or combine Buddha and World-Honored One into one. The variations differ. Because the sutras say that the Buddha possesses ten titles, the number ten is taken as the standard. Only the Great Treatise, counting from Tathagata first to Buddha tenth, divides them into ten, and takes World-Honored One as the collective name of the ten titles, which seems most fitting.

“At the hour for the meal.” It is the fixed rule of the Buddhas of the three periods that once the middle of the day has passed, one may not eat. Here it means that the hour for the meal was approaching, and so he should go to beg first. In the vinaya of the Tripitaka, the accounts of the hour for the meal are not uniform. Let one account be given here. The hours of the ox, the tiger, and the hare are the mealtime of the gods, and are called the first division. (Some say the hours of the tiger, the hare, and the dragon are the first division; the Essentials of Guifeng follow this account.) The hours of the dragon, the snake, and the horse are the mealtime of humans, and are called the middle division. The hours of the sheep, the monkey, and the rooster are the mealtime of animals, and are called the afternoon division. The hours of the dog, the boar, and the rat are the mealtime of spirits and ghosts, and are called the night division. The meaning is that the beings of each path mostly eat at these times, or that these times are suitable for eating, not that it is absolutely fixed. Only the Buddha-Dharma institutes not eating after noon. The intent is deep and broad, as stated in the vinaya. The time for begging was roughly around the hour of the dragon, because if too early or too late one could not obtain food; one guards against there being no giver, which would trouble others, and against obtaining nothing, which would trouble oneself.

“Put on his robe.” The Buddha instituted the three robes. First, the antarvasa, meaning the robe worn within; it is worn against the body. It may be used when walking the Way (that is, when cultivating) or when working. This is the five-strip robe, called the lower-grade robe. Second, the uttarasanga, translated as “upper robe,” also called the middle-grade robe. This is the seven-strip robe. One may also enter a village or teach the Dharma in it. If one meets a great assembly, one should wear the great robe. Third, the samghati, meaning the robe worn when the assembly gathers; this is the great robe. It is also called the upper-grade robe, and also the field-of-merit robe. It is the nine-strip robe up to the twenty-five-strip robe. If one enters a royal palace, a royal city, or a village, or wherever a great assembly gathers and the deportment is solemn — or when conferring precepts, teaching the Dharma, or begging for food — one should wear this robe. From five strips to nine strips, in every case the cloth is cut into squares, sewn and joined; when the number of strips is few, the squares are large; when the number of strips is many, the squares are small. When small, they are dense like the clearly drawn boundaries of a field, and therefore only the nine-strip robe is called the field-of-merit robe. Above ten strips, since there are those whose bodies are stalwart, the robe's measure is correspondingly broad, and so the number of strips increases. In the cold lands of India, the three robes may be worn layered. In the Eastern Land, because of cold and of custom, most simply add the robe over ordinary clothing, and so there is no custom of layering; only among the lamas does it exist. The three robes are collectively called kashaya. Kashaya is Sanskrit, and is named by way of color, meaning a color that is improper, spoiled, or turbid. Hence by extension a mixed taste is also called the kashaya taste. “Improper” makes clear that it is mixed. When colors are mixed, the color is spoiled and turbid. Therefore black must be like mud; blue should resemble bronze-blue (the color of old bronze); red is either red with little black, called the color of lotus-tree bark (there is such a tree in Sichuan; in Japan it is called incense-dyed color, dyed with clove), which is what India calls the gandha color, or red and black intermixed like purple. The Record of Returning from the Western Regions says: “Either take chips of rehmannia, or yellow from vitex and cypress, grind red earth and red stone into juice, blend and dye with it.” In sum, one is not permitted to use the bright, pure colors of blue, yellow, red, black, and purple. One must mix in other colors and make them dim and turbid. The Four-Part Vinaya says: “In each and every color, spoil it as one pleases” — this is the meaning. As for the plain-strip robe, it is the robe of novice monks and novice nuns, meaning that it is undivided with no sign of strips. Great monks who lack the three robes may use it generally. Laymen and laywomen are also permitted to borrow and wear it temporarily when worshipping the Buddha and the like; they may not wear it regularly. When the Buddha-Dharma first came east, those who had left home did not know the rule of cutting and joining, and merely wore the plain-strip robe. Only after a hundred and eighty-seven years had passed did they come to know it.

“Took up his bowl.” In Sanskrit, patra; this is rendered as “the vessel according to measure.” It means that the food should accord with the measure, not too large, so as to restrain greed. It is also said that body, color, and measure should all accord with Dharma. The body is limited to iron, clay, and the like; wooden ones are not permitted, because outsiders use them and because they easily hold greasy dirt. The color is plain. The measure is as said above. Abbreviated as “the vessel according to measure,” it means the vessel worthy of offerings by sages and holy ones. When Shakyamuni attained the Way, the four heavenly kings took the sapphire-blue stone bowl of the past Buddha Vishvabhu, which was offered in the dragon palace, and transformed it into four; each presented one. The World-Honored One then joined the four into one and used it to beg for food.

“Entered the great city of Shravasti.” The garden was five or six li southeast of the city, and so it says he entered the city. The city was more than sixty li in circumference. In the inner city there were nine hundred million households; the land was broad and the people dense, and so it is called “great.”

“To beg for food.” The Buddha instituted that those who have left home are not permitted to use four methods to seek food and sustain life. First, planting and cultivating, called “food of the downward mouth.” Second, observing the stars to speak of fortune and misfortune, called “food of the upward mouth.” Third, trafficking with the powerful in the four directions, called “food of the directional mouth.” Fourth, divining good and ill fortune and the like, called “food of the webbing mouth.” These are collectively called impure food, food of wrong livelihood. Only begging is permitted, and is called food of right livelihood. This is the right way for one who has left home. What is the right way? It is because it breaks down pride, because it does not crave the palate, because it concentrates the mind on walking the Way, and because it causes all people to break their stinginess and increase their merit. As for the Buddha himself begging for food, according to the Sutra of the Necklace of Pearls it contains many meanings: for instance, causing all people not to give rise to arrogance; causing all obstructed sentient beings to see the Buddha and obtain benefit; and displaying to those who have left home that they should not accumulate stores.

“In that city, having begged in order from house to house.” “In order” means begging from house to house successively, without picking and choosing. “Having begged” means either the bowl was filled to the brim, or one stopped at the seventh house; it does not mean that he begged in order through the whole city. Joined with the sentence that follows: as soon as the begging was done he returned, without looking back a little.
“Returned to his original place.” From the city he returned to the garden.

“When the meal was finished.” “Meal” means to eat, as in the Analects, “to eat coarse food.” “Finished” means done. The Sutra of the Jewel Cloud says that the food obtained by begging is divided into four parts: one part to be given to fellow practitioners of the pure life; one part to be given in charity to the poor, the sick, and beggars; one part to be given to beings of water and land; and one part kept for oneself. The Sutra of the Twelve Ascetic Practices does not speak of giving to fellow practitioners of the pure life. Each has its intent, and they should be combined in practice. That it is not mentioned there is because all should beg for themselves; that it is mentioned here is because some may have other circumstances and no leisure to beg. Here, as to the two kinds, fellow practitioners of the pure life and the poor and sick, it says “to be given” and “to be given in charity,” making clear that it is not fixed, and that if there are such one gives to them. As for beings of water and land, one should certainly give, and so it does not say “to be given,” but simply states it.
“Put away his robe and bowl.” If he did not put them away, he could not avoid keeping them in mind, and could not set his mind at ease to cultivate the Way.

“Washed his feet.” It was to protect living beings that he walked barefoot to beg. (In India people commonly wear leather sandals, which easily harm living creatures.) Fearing that he might be stained with dust, he had to wash them. Joined with the sentence that follows: when the matter was done he at once cultivated contemplation, taking the Way as weighty.

“Spread his seat and sat down.” “Spread the seat”: “spread” means to unfold; “seat” means the sitting mat. Among the four deportments of walking, standing, sitting, and lying, walking easily gives rise to restlessness, standing easily to fatigue, and lying easily to torpor. For the cultivator only sitting is supreme, and therefore many who have left home do not lie down at all. Sitting cross-legged is the common form in the Buddha's gate, and so it is not mentioned in detail here. Cross-legged sitting has four benefits: first, body and mind are gathered and collected, and lightness and ease quickly arise; second, one can endure for a long time without quickly tiring; third, it is not shared with outsiders, who have no such method; fourth, the bearing is dignified and weighty, arousing the reverence and faith of others.

From the putting on of the robe above to the sitting down, all of it was our Buddha's compassion, bending down to set an example for the great assembly. The World-Honored One had no need to do so at all. How is this shown? As the Sutra of the Girl with the Necklace says, the transformation-Buddha's body is like a single mass of vajra, without the two organs of digestion. The Nirvana Sutra says: the Tathagata's body is not a body fed on mixed food; why should he need to beg? That he displayed begging — besides the three meanings already given above of causing all people not to give rise to arrogance — was nothing other than to set a model for cultivators. Since he had no need to eat, and yet it says “when the meal was finished,” one does not know whether he actually ate or not. There are two meanings here. First, if he did not eat at all, the giver's merit would not be complete; in his compassion the Buddha causes him to fulfill his vow, and so he too often ate along with the assembly. Second, some say that when the food was about to reach his mouth, a god of awesome virtue stood invisibly at his side and received it away to another region, to be offered in the Buddha's work. Thus the Buddha both displayed eating, causing the giver's merit to be complete, and by spiritual power removed it for the Buddha's work. So eating and not eating — the two meanings do not obstruct each other. Again the Agama Sutra says that when the Buddha walked he rose four fingers' breadth above the ground, with lotus flowers bearing his feet, so that he had no need to wash them. Yet here he displayed all these circumstances one by one; was this not bending down to be a model for the great assembly?

The first passage spoken above was nothing more than dissolving the meaning according to the words. What was said in the second passage, about being a model for people, is likewise a general meaning. The most essential thing is to understand why this sutra sets forth such circumstances as its opening. One should know that herein lies a great and subtle meaning. This is precisely an intimate pointing, requiring people to realize it amid their going and stopping, their movement and stillness. Consider: the Tathagata, for the sake of saving sentient beings, though not born yet appearing to be born, showed himself the same as an ordinary man. On what day did he not put on his robe and eat, that is, on what day was he not setting an example by his own person? Why is it that the beginning of most sutras records the emitting of light and the shaking of the earth? Now, wishing to proclaim the supreme dharani of all Dharmas, the great Dharma of the Diamond Prajna that gives birth to all Buddhas, he yet chose to record this passage of ordinary daily affairs as the opening. Is it not strange? Is it not wondrous? The wonder is not in the wondrous place; the wonder is in the coarse and shallow place. One should know that the most ordinary matters and the most profound principle are intimately related. The various commentators ancient and modern either saw the precepts and concentration as the opening, or took the scene of unmoving suchness as the opening, or said that daily matters must not be looked upon lightly, or said that putting on the robe and eating is itself the emitting of light and shaking of the earth. Each had what he saw, and each possesses its own wonder. Here I have selectively adopted these accounts, and further, from the side of the essential purport that bears directly on the sutra text, adduced proof and made it clear, so that people may more easily grasp it. The meaning is deep, and cannot be exhausted in a moment. Let it be summarized in ten layers and spoken of in rough outline.

(1) Prajna is the essential Dharma for nourishing the life of wisdom and for continuing and prospering the Buddha-seed. It is like food and clothing, which are the essential matters by which people of the world sustain the body of form and carry on from those before and pass on to those after. Now this putting on the robe and begging and the rest are taken as the opening precisely to make those who have brought forth the great aspiration understand that this Dharma-food of prajna cannot be parted from for even a moment. Therefore the sutra says: “Those who receive and uphold, read and recite, and widely expound it for others bear the supreme bodhi.” It also says: “One should know that such a person accomplishes the supreme, foremost, and rarest Dharma.” It also says: “Wherever this sutra is, there is the Buddha, or a revered disciple.” Viewed from the reverse side of these few passages, one may solemnly see that it is the same as food and clothing: its bearing is very great, and it cannot be parted from even briefly. Therefore it is taken as the opening.

(2) The sutra says: “In the last five hundred years there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit, and who can give rise to faith in these chapter-phrases.” One may see that upholding the precepts and cultivating merit is the gate by which prajna enters the Way. Begging for food is instituted by the precepts. Now displaying the putting on of the robe, the taking up of the bowl, and the begging in order, is both leading sentient beings to uphold the precepts and universally causing sentient beings to cultivate merit. This is what the sutra's verse means: “The Dharmakaya is fundamentally not food, and the response-body is likewise so; to increase the merit of gods and humans, in compassion he becomes a field of merit.” That the World-Honored One begged for food day after day was, day after day, setting forth in sentient beings a root of faith capable of entering prajna. Now, before he wished to teach the Diamond Prajna, he recorded this as the opening: how intimate it is.

(3) Master Guifeng said: the precepts can assist concentration, and concentration can bring forth wisdom; therefore he takes the precepts and concentration as the opening. One should know that wisdom without precepts and concentration is wild wisdom, not right wisdom. Begging for food is the precepts; spreading the seat and sitting down is for entering concentration. Having displayed the circumstances of precepts and concentration, he then speaks the profound prajna. Is this not displaying the definite sequence of the three studies and making people know what comes first and what after? Further, the sutra speaks only of wisdom, and so in the opening he specifically supplies the precepts and concentration. How earnest and thorough are the Buddhas and bodhisattvas in saving sentient beings — just so, just so.

(4) For every student, to be able to train amid food, clothing, rising, and resting, in the dust of toil, is the most essential method for subduing the deluded mind. For to crave food and clothing and to shrink from no toil is assuredly to grasp at appearances; yet to resent the toil and give rise to affliction is also to grasp at appearances. One must meet circumstances and follow conditions, neither deluded nor vexed: this is the method of pacifying the mind. Therefore the sutra says: “All Dharmas are the Buddha-Dharma.” The sutra also often speaks of subduing and dwelling in terms of the perfections such as giving; this too is the meaning. Consider: among us ordinary beings, who does not want food and clothing? One cannot shake them off, and one cannot gratify one's greed for them. And since one has brought forth the great aspiration to learn the Buddha's Way, such matters as giving and saving living beings must all be learned. If one does not exert effort in all of this being such, then from morning to night one either grasps at existence or grasps at emptiness, and when will one ever find a single moment of ease? Even a single recitation of the Buddha's name cannot be done well, and the work of spreading the Dharma and benefiting living beings cannot be learned well either. Now, upon clothing and eating, he sets forth the profound prajna of not grasping at either extreme and of all being such, causing people to realize that they should exert effort precisely upon such circumstances. One must not cling to existence and obscure emptiness, grasping at Dharma-appearance; still less may one depart from existence and speak of emptiness, grasping at no-Dharma-appearance. Truly great compassion and great pity.

(5) That the Tathagata accorded with ordinary beings, putting on his robe and begging for food, makes clear that he did not grasp at the appearance of the fruit-stage. This is precisely what the sutra says: “The Tathagata means the suchness of all Dharmas.” One should know that if the fruit is such, the cause is also such. Therefore one should detach from all appearances and bring forth the aspiration for supreme enlightenment. And the method of subduing is wholly contained therein. By the non-grasping of the fruit-virtue, he sets forth that the causal practice should not grasp at appearances. This is truly what is called the cause encompassing the ocean of fruit, and the fruit penetrating to the source of the cause. How wondrous, how wondrous.

(6) The Sutra of the Golden Light, Supreme King of Kings says: the five aggregates are the Dharmakaya. The five aggregates are illusory existence born of conditions; the Dharmakaya is the true emptiness of stillness and illumination. This is to tell people that they should, precisely within illusory existence, see true emptiness, and not fall into annihilation. This sutra's many dismissals of appearance, which come to rest in the Dharma's not speaking of annihilation, have the same meaning. One should know that what is called the emptiness of the ultimate meaning requires precisely that one neither grasp nor annihilate; only then is it called the ultimate meaning. This is the crucial point in learning prajna. And that the Tathagata displayed the Dharmakaya in the illusory appearances of an ordinary man's food and clothing is precisely to have ordinary beings recognize, upon each one's own illusory appearances, the Dharmakaya they inherently possess. Only do not chase the deluded; why seek the true outside the deluded? If one grasps at the true, then within the true delusion arises. In the sutra, such passages as “one should give rise to a mind that does not abide, and yet give rise to that mind,” “one should give rise to a mind that does not abide,” “ordinary beings are not ordinary beings,” and “sentient beings are not sentient beings” — all of them explain the meaning of neither grasping nor annihilating, neither approaching nor departing. If so, then this sutra's opening may be called most apt and essential.

(7) The Tathagata displayed begging for food, and having begged, at once returned to his original place. We ordinary beings only know how to busy ourselves seeking food; all day and all year we chase outward, and never once think of turning the light back upon our own nature. Again, the Tathagata displayed that when the meal was done he at once put everything away, gathered himself in stillness, and entered contemplation. We ordinary beings, by contrast, play after eating our fill and are restless without cease; when have we ever been still for a single moment, let alone able to cultivate contemplation? One should know that the power of prajna-wisdom is born of inward illumination, and inward illumination requires first the gathering of stillness. The use of these sentences as the opening precisely points out to us that when any worldly condition comes we should meet it, and when the matter is past we should put it away and cast it aside; then, returning to quiet contemplation, turning from dust and joining with enlightenment, only then can the fundamental wisdom of prajna be set forth. Take note, take note.

(8) The essential purport of the whole Diamond Sutra lies only in “how to subdue” and “how to dwell.” Yet how easy is that to speak of? Master Datian said: “The moment there is something dwelt in, the mind of enlightenment perishes. Just when one wishes to subdue, the deluded mind blazes up the more.” Therefore one must subdue without subduing and dwell without dwelling. But how does one begin? Now observe the World-Honored One putting on his robe and eating, walking the streets and passing the lanes, washing his feet and spreading his seat — trifling and petty matters, and not so for a single time only. For forty-nine years of saving living beings, for forty-nine years it was thus. Though the vajra body had no need of food, no need to wash its feet, and no need to learn concentration, yet for the sake of sentient beings he practiced it day after day, acting without affair — truly equal and such. This passage of native scenery is itself the great model of subduing the mind and dwelling the mind. We must cultivate and learn accordingly. Whenever a circumstance comes, we should practice according to the teaching, acting without affair. Acting without affair is precisely subduing without subduing and dwelling without dwelling. In this way perhaps one may enter into accord with the profound purport of prajna.

(9) It is to be feared that what was said above of subduing without subduing and dwelling without dwelling is still not understood. Let it be said again. The World-Honored One was utterly unlike others; why did he display the ways of an ordinary man and differ not at all from others? One should know that it is just because he differed not at all from others that he was utterly unlike others. We should realize this from this point, and realize it upon our own persons. Why? Because although we are ordinary beings, we inherently possess the such Buddha-nature. Why? Because we do not grasp at appearances. In learning prajna, we should exert effort in not grasping at appearances. Not grasping means not departing from all appearances, yet not grasping them. If one one-sidedly takes no-appearance as non-grasping, then one again grasps at no-Dharma-appearance and falls into annihilation. Therefore the sutra says: “If one sees all appearances as no-appearance, then one sees the Tathagata.” “All appearances as no-appearance” means that although there are all appearances, one does not grasp them. It also says: “Not grasping at appearances, unmoving suchness.” It is precisely because one does not grasp that one can see all Dharma-appearances and no-Dharma-appearances. Not grasping is precisely subduing without subduing and dwelling without dwelling. That the sutra opens with not grasping at appearances as the setting forth — its purport is deep.

(10) Gathering together all that has been said above, one may see that the whole section of setting forth fully reveals the emptiness of the ultimate meaning. See how the Tathagata showed himself as an ordinary man only for the sake of benefiting others: this is no self-appearance. The wondrous Dharma of prajna, spontaneously flowing freely from trifling matters of circumstance: this is no Dharma-appearance. Needing no food yet going to beg, even manifesting the washing of feet and the spreading of the seat, and by the teaching that is not spoken protecting in thought and entrusting all who have brought forth the great aspiration: this too is no no-Dharma-appearance. If one can comprehend this, true emptiness and its principle and wisdom stand plainly before the mind's eye. Whose exposition of the setting forth could surpass this in precision?

You should know, gentlemen, that the reason I have spoken again and again upon the section of setting forth, not daring to shrink from prolixity, is nothing else: I wish to enable all good friends to know how faith is brought forth, and to understand clearly the principle and wisdom of the three emptinesses, which may be seen in every matter. One should, when putting on clothes and eating, when walking and stopping, moving and resting, at all times contemplate in this way, and one may then obtain benefit at once. Only then will one know that the whole Diamond Sutra is truly a good prescription for removing suffering and adversity, and a shortcut into the Buddha's wisdom. Revere it! Revere it!

(J) Next, the orthodox division, in two parts: (K) first, the one at the moment praises and requests; next, the Tathagata praises and permits. (K) First, again in two: (L) first, bowing in praise; next, requesting the Dharma. (L) First, again in two: (M) first, arranging the deportment; next, offering praise.
(M) First, arranging the deportment.

[At that time the elder Subhuti rose from his seat in the midst of the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and spoke to the Buddha:]

“At that time” refers precisely to the time when the World-Honored One had begged for food and returned to the garden. This word “time” should be eyed most carefully. The exclamation of “how rare” below comes right on the heels of the passage above about putting on the robe and taking up the bowl. That the compiler of the sutra set down the word “time” contains within it boundless feeling. The World-Honored One put on his robe, took up his bowl, and begged for food, and it was so day after day, so that the assembly saw it as if not seeing it. This time the conditions had ripened, and so Subhuti alone saw through it at a glance. The great Dharma of prajna the World-Honored One did not often teach; and even when he taught it, he had to wait until the conditions had ripened. This is truly rare and hard to meet, what is called once in a thousand years.

“Elder” is a title for one honored both in years and in virtue. The Tang translation has “endowed with life,” showing only his advanced age. The Wei translation has “life of wisdom,” showing only the length of his virtue. Kumarajiva, following the literary sense of this land, translated it as “elder,” which contains both meanings.

Subhuti is also translated as “Born of Emptiness,” and also as “Well Appearing” and “Well Auspicious.” His household was rich in wealth and treasure, and at the time of his birth the gold and silver in the family storehouses were all emptied; therefore he was called Born of Emptiness. Seven days after his birth the treasures in the storehouse reappeared; therefore he was called Well Appearing. Again, a physiognomist divined and said: “This child is well auspicious; there is no need for concern”; therefore he was called Well Auspicious. That the storehouse was empty at his first birth displays the principle of emptiness. That the treasures afterward reappeared displays that emptiness is not one-sided emptiness. The Records of the Western Regions say: Subhuti was originally the Buddha Dragon-Knot of the eastern region, who projected a reflection into Shakyamuni's assembly, manifesting the trace of an arhat to assist Shakyamuni in his teaching. In the Buddha's gate he was foremost in understanding emptiness. Empty yet not empty — only this is true emptiness, only this is the emptiness of the ultimate meaning. The other disciples were not so deeply awakened as Subhuti, and therefore at the prajna assembly Subhuti was necessarily the one at the moment, to ask on behalf of the great assembly.

That Subhuti requested on behalf of the great assembly contains four essential meanings. (1) The ordinary members of the assembly saw the World-Honored One day after day putting on his robe and taking up his bowl, the same as any ordinary monk who begged for food, and were utterly at a loss as to what his intent was. Therefore it had to be Subhuti, who manifested the trace of a hearer, who requested on their behalf. (2) This was already the ninth assembly, and the World-Honored One, in the midst of ordinary dressing and eating, was well protecting in thought and well entrusting the great Dharma of prajna, bringing out the deepest principle of the emptiness of the ultimate meaning wholly and completely. The assembly of course could not understand it, and none but Subhuti could request it on their behalf. (3) The elders in the Buddha's gate were not Subhuti alone. But since none understood emptiness as he did, the one at the moment to request the Dharma could only be Subhuti. (4) There were also bodhisattva-mahasattvas in the assembly; why did they not request, but let Subhuti ask alone? Because the Buddha taught prajna primarily for the arhats, and secondarily for the bodhisattvas. If a bodhisattva had requested, the arhats might have doubted that this was the Dharma of bodhisattvas and had nothing to do with them. Now, letting Subhuti request, this doubt could be prevented. Subhuti's request was entirely for the sake of the great assembly, and below, as soon as he opens his mouth, he speaks of good men and good women. Therefore the phrase “in the midst of the great assembly” contains many meanings. “Then and there” (ji) means “at once,” with a sense of not being able to wait. The World-Honored One had spread his seat and sat down, and the assembly likewise; therefore Subhuti rose from his seat at once. Spoken from the trace, it is thus. Spoken from the root, Subhuti had long since become a Buddha, and the World-Honored One had already taught prajna eight times. Why must he wait until the ninth teaching of the Diamond Prajna before rising from his seat to ask? One may see that in every matter the four — time, season, cause, and condition — must all be complete before it can come together. The World-Honored One's teaching of prajna is the time; the teaching of the Diamond Prajna is the season; there are various causes and various conditions; and when at this point causes and conditions were complete, Subhuti then, as the one at the moment, asked about this great Dharma. The kashaya robe was on the left shoulder, and so the right shoulder could be bared. By the Buddha's institution, the kashaya was not normally worn bared; only when being reverent was it bared. When people do work they must use the right hand, and when walking they put the right foot forward first: this expresses the meaning that a disciple who has a task performs the labor. This sutra lays its weight on bearing supreme bodhi, and so disciples should rightly take this responsibility upon their shoulders. When worshipping, both knees are placed on the ground. In repentance one kneels on the right knee, which the ancients called kneeling in the foreign manner. “On the ground” means with the feet planted on solid ground, displaying that the Dharma is the ground of actual principle, that is, true suchness, causing one to realize the original nature. “Joined his palms” means the two palms pressed together, grasping at no outer thing. Our two hands pull east and west, all of it dust and defilement; now joining them is turning from dust and joining with enlightenment. From baring the shoulder to joining the palms is the purification of bodily karma. An upright and grave outward appearance is called reverence; inner sincerity and respect is called veneration — this is the purification of mental karma. And “spoke to the Buddha”: “spoke” means to declare, to declare one's own meaning outwardly — this is the purification of verbal karma. All of the above are the words of the compiler of the sutra.
(M) Next, offering praise.
[“How rare, World-Honored One! The Tathagata well protects in thought all bodhisattvas and well entrusts all bodhisattvas.”]

It is usually said “how rare.” Summed up, there are four meanings: first, rare in time, because the Tathagata's appearing in the world is hard to meet even in vast kalpas; second, rare in place, because in the three thousand great thousand worlds there is only one Buddha; third, rare in virtue, because his merit and wisdom are supreme and unequalled; fourth, rare in deed, because his compassion and skillful means are the most ingenious. The above four are the common account. Here, the “how rare” refers precisely to prajna-paramita. “World-Honored One” is the general title, used in address. To call him “Buddha” expresses the fruit-virtue; to call him “Tathagata” expresses the nature-virtue. Subhuti, in the Buddha's putting on his robe and eating and the rest, saw all appearances as no-appearance, and so saw the Tathagata; therefore as soon as he opened his mouth he called him Tathagata. This venerable one, by the Dharmakaya Tathagata, displayed himself as an ordinary man: this is precisely displaying that he does not abide in any appearance. Why did the Dharmakaya Tathagata show himself the same as an ordinary man? Precisely because he does not abandon sentient beings; this is protecting in thought. Not abandoning sentient beings is great compassion. And to display it by the Dharmakaya Tathagata is great wisdom. This great compassion is born of great wisdom: it is existent yet not existent. Existent yet not existent is precisely wondrous existence, precisely the wondrous existence that does not obstruct true emptiness. To protect in thought by a wondrous existence that does not obstruct true emptiness — is this not “well”? To manifest a trace the same as an ordinary man is precisely to display the Dharmakaya Tathagata's not abiding in any appearance. The essential meaning of the Diamond Prajna is wholly brought out; this is entrusting by the teaching that is not spoken. The teaching that is not spoken is great wisdom. This great wisdom is born of great compassion: it is empty yet not empty. Empty yet not empty is precisely true emptiness, precisely the true emptiness that does not obstruct wondrous existence. To entrust by a true emptiness that does not obstruct wondrous existence — no “well” could be better than this. Whether protecting in thought or entrusting, it is nothing but the twofold revelation of emptiness and existence. The whole sutra sets forth the profound principle of true emptiness and wondrous existence, and this may be seen everywhere. Understand this, and the veins and threads run through. The exclamation of “how rare” is indeed the meaning of hard to meet even in vast kalpas, yet it also contains the meaning of hard to comprehend. This may be verified from the following passages: “From of old until now, the wisdom-eye I have attained has never heard such a sutra as this,” and “I now hear such a sutra, and believe, understand, receive, and uphold it; this is not hard. But in a future age, in the last five hundred years, if there are sentient beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, receive, and uphold it, such a person will be foremost and rarest.” All of these can prove how difficult belief and understanding are. Subhuti means: from of old until now I have only just now seen the Tathagata's protecting in thought and entrusting. Though the assembly cannot comprehend it, the World-Honored One always displayed it thus, and this is all the more rare. As for protecting in thought and entrusting, why are both said to be “well”? Protecting in thought belongs to the mind; entrusting belongs to the mouth. If one waited to arouse the mind in order to protect in thought, then one would protect in thought only when the mind was aroused, and not when it was not. If one waited to speak in order to entrust, then there would be entrusting only when one spoke, and none when one did not. Neither could be called “well.” Now, by the Tathagata's entering the city and returning to the garden, unmoving suchness, he secretly shows the dwelling of the mind and sets an example by his own person: this is precisely protecting and remembering. And by his sitting in repose after the meal, with not a single thought arising, he secretly shows the subduing of the mind, causing the assembly to take it as their model: this is precisely entrusting with earnest admonition. Between movement and stillness, he teaches by his person and not by his words. At all times and in all places he is a model for bodhisattvas: this is truly what is called “well.” That Subhuti opened his mouth and sighed “how rare” was indeed well founded.
(L) Next, requesting the Dharma.
[“World-Honored One, when good men and good women bring forth the aspiration for supreme, perfectly equal, perfect enlightenment, how should they dwell? How should they subdue their minds?”]
The common editions read “how should they dwell.” Here, following the Tang manuscript edition, it reads “how should they dwell.”

The “bodhisattvas” of the passage above refers precisely to these good men and good women. Because they bring forth the supreme aspiration, they have the qualifications for Buddhahood and may be called bodhisattvas. “Good” means good roots. To bring forth the supreme aspiration, one cannot do so without great good roots. Everyone has good roots; without good roots one could not be born among humans, nor hear this great Dharma. Yet if one does not bring forth the aspiration, one merely holds these good roots in vain — does one not then fail them? In the Buddhist sutras women are often rebuked. It is also often said that women have heavy obstructions and cannot become Buddhas, and must first be transformed into a male body. Some doubt that if the Buddha-Dharma is equal, then requiring a woman first to become a man is inequality. Such people do not understand the Buddha's principle but criticize the Buddha-Dharma first, which is greatly impermissible. In sum, women indeed have heavy obstructions: first, the obstruction of childbirth; second, they often mistake attachment for compassion. Compassion is equal, from the first without closeness or distance, thickness or thinness. Attachment is the river of birth and death; misapplied, it falls into rebirth. In the Buddha's eye there is from the first no appearance of man or woman; therefore to say that women have heavy obstructions is to have them pay special attention and not be subject to this obstruction. One need only bring forth the great aspiration, and one becomes a Buddha just the same. This is why Subhuti asked both questions. “Bring forth” means to produce, to arouse. It means to arouse the mind that seeks the Buddha's Way above and transforms sentient beings below, aspiring to realize the supreme fruit. The word “bring forth” runs through the passage above and below, and its meaning covers both the active and the passive: the good men and good women above are the ones who bring forth, and the supreme enlightenment and the rest below are what is brought forth.

In Sanskrit, anuttara is rendered here as “supreme”; samyak, as “perfectly equal”; sambodhi, as “perfect enlightenment.” Together: supreme, perfectly equal, perfect enlightenment. “Perfect enlightenment” distinguishes it from the incorrect enlightenment of ordinary people and outsiders; for ordinary people, having a self, cannot enlighten themselves, and outsiders may have enlightenment but it belongs to the one-sided and erroneous, and is not perfect enlightenment. “Perfectly equal” distinguishes it from the inequality of the two vehicles; the arhats all attain perfect enlightenment, yet they dread birth and death as a prison, are eager to save themselves, lack the mind of compassion, cannot cultivate good and save living beings, and so have no mind of equality. “Perfectly equal” refers precisely to bodhisattvas. “Perfectly equal” means enlightening oneself and enlightening others, self and other equally. “Supreme” distinguishes it from the bodhisattva's having something above him. The bodhisattva's enlightenment, though perfectly equal, is still not the Buddha's perfect completion of enlightenment and practice. “Supreme” refers precisely to the Buddha. What these good men and good women bring forth is precisely the Buddha's supreme mind of enlightenment. The mind is the essence of spiritual clarity and illumined awareness; in its function it divides into true and deluded, defiled and pure. Here, bringing it forth in reliance on bodhi plainly shows it to be true and pure, not deluded and defiled. The Great Treatise says: from cause to fruit there are five kinds of bodhi. First, the bodhi of bringing forth the aspiration, which is the stage of the ten faiths. Second, the bodhi of subduing the mind, which is the stage of the three worthy ones. Third, the bodhi of clarifying the mind, which is from the first ground to the seventh. Fourth, the bodhi of going forth and arriving, which is from the eighth ground to the tenth. Fifth, supreme bodhi, which is the Tathagata's fruit-stage. Here, as to the one who brings forth the aspiration, it corresponds to the first; as to the aspiration brought forth, it corresponds to the fifth. Discussing the active and the passive together, it runs through both beginning and end. Thus one knows that “supreme” belongs to the fruit, and “perfectly equal, perfect enlightenment” belongs to the cause; and the mind that is brought forth runs through both cause and fruit. “Should” means ought; this word runs through the two sentences that follow. “Dwell” means to rest in one place. “Subdue” means to control and gather in. The word “mind” in “their minds” refers to the deluded and defiled. The question has three meanings: anyone who is a bodhisattva must bring forth the bodhi-mind, and so he first asks about bringing forth the aspiration. Having first brought forth this mind, one cannot dwell as the Buddha does, following conditions in peace, and so he next asks about dwelling the mind. His intent is to seek the Buddha's instruction in a method by which this mind can be brought into accord and dwell. And because the deluded mind arises repeatedly and cannot be subdued as naturally as the Buddha's, he next asks about subduing. His intent is to seek the Buddha's instruction in a method by which the deluded mind can be subdued naturally.

Bringing forth the aspiration comes first. Yet one must bring forth the great aspiration before one can practice the great practices and attain the great fruit. The Avatamsaka Sutra says: “One who forgets and loses the bodhi-mind and cultivates good fruits is held by maras.” When good men and women first bring forth the aspiration, they should at once set Buddhahood as their aim and bring forth the aspiration for supreme, perfectly equal, perfect enlightenment. “Supreme” is precisely what is sought. To seek the supreme, one must cultivate merit and save living beings; therefore next it says “perfectly equal.” To save living beings, one should first save oneself; therefore next it says “perfect enlightenment.” Spoken in reverse order, it is self-enlightened, enlightening others, and complete in enlightenment and practice.
