The treatise says: “The initial aspiration and the ultimate are not two; of these two minds, the initial is the hard one.” The bodhi of bringing forth the aspiration and supreme bodhi are one mind, not two. Yet the initial bringing forth is hard, and therefore Subhuti first raised bringing forth the aspiration as his question. Dwelling and subduing come after. Some have previously brought forth the aspiration and afterward forgotten and lost it: this is not knowing how the true mind should be peacefully dwelt in, so that the deluded mind cannot be subdued. Therefore the youth Sudhana, whenever he met a good friend, would always request: “I have already brought forth the aspiration for supreme, perfectly equal, perfect enlightenment, but I do not yet know how to learn the bodhisattva's practices and cultivate the bodhisattva's path.” Thus one knows that one who brings forth the great aspiration must practice the great practices. Dwelling and subduing are precisely the practical point of taking up genuine cultivation. Therefore he next asks about dwelling and subduing. Yet these two questions in truth support each other: when the mind of enlightenment dwells, the deluded mind is subdued without subduing; when the deluded mind is subdued, the mind of enlightenment dwells without dwelling.
(K) Next, the Tathagata praises and permits. Again in two: (L) first, praising and confirming; next, permitting the teaching.
(L) First, praising and confirming.
[The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent. Subhuti, as you have said, the Tathagata well protects in thought all bodhisattvas and well entrusts all bodhisattvas.”]

That the compiler of the sutra set the word “Buddha” here has a deep meaning. “Buddha” is the fruit of ultimate enlightenment; the one who brought forth the aspiration above is precisely cultivating the cause. To know the road down the mountain, one must ask one who has come from there. The word “Buddha” placed here means: as is the cause, so is the fruit; and conversely, as is the fruit, so is the cause. “Excellent, excellent” is praise. “As you have said” is confirmation. The first “excellent” praises his having well accorded with the Tathagata's original mind. For several decades he had displayed the dust of toil, silently protecting in thought and entrusting, without ever a word spoken; now Subhuti alone could see it, and so he praises him. The second “excellent” praises his requesting on behalf of the assembly. The Buddha's painstaking mind was precisely that good men and women should bring forth the aspiration and go to learn; yet no one could request it. Now Subhuti alone could ask, to fulfill the Tathagata's original vow, and so he praises him again. Others could not ask; you alone could ask: therefore the first “excellent” praises his great wisdom. He asked the Dharma not for himself but for the great assembly: therefore the second “excellent” praises his great compassion. You could truly see my not abiding in the Buddha-appearance, and my protecting in thought and entrusting; therefore it says “as you have said.” For thus protecting in thought and entrusting the great assembly could not understand, and Subhuti alone could point it out; therefore he confirms his words. The two phrases about the Tathagata were originally Subhuti's words of praise to the Buddha. Now the Buddha wholeheartedly accepts them, saying that the Tathagata's protecting in thought and entrusting is as you have said, not the least bit wrong. This is to cause sentient beings, amid the Tathagata's putting on his robe, taking up his bowl, coming and going, moving and resting, to receive and grasp the meaning of protecting in thought and entrusting.

(L) Next, permitting the teaching. Again in two: (M) first, the general indication; next, the detailed discourse. (M) First, again in two: (N) first, admonishing to listen and marking the doctrine; next, according with the purport and requesting detail.
(N) First, admonishing to listen and marking the doctrine.
[“Now listen attentively; I will teach you. Good men and good women who bring forth the aspiration for supreme, perfectly equal, perfect enlightenment should thus dwell and thus subdue their minds.”]

How could Subhuti fail to listen attentively? The Buddha's admonition was for the assembly and for us sentient beings now. “Attentive” means true and correct. First, one must not be arrogant; second, one must not belittle oneself. If one falls into these two faults, one cannot listen attentively, and even hearing, one cannot be correct. Some who have studied the treatises a little think themselves versed in Buddhist learning: this is the fault of arrogance. Some exalt the sagely realm on high, thinking that with such a great Dharma how could we understand it: this is the fault of self-belittlement. Arrogance is pride; self-belittlement is also a low pride. Listening to the sutra thus, one cannot be true and correct. Therefore students of the Buddha's Way must rid themselves of these two faults and receive with an empty mind; hence “listen attentively.” Since one can listen attentively, how could he not speak? Therefore he says, “I will teach you,” meaning: if you did not listen attentively, I would not teach you. These words spur us on: when hearing the sutra, all one's former knowledge and views must be wholly set aside and not kept in the mind. The three phrases from “good men and good women” onward precisely mark out the essential purport of the practice. The old explanation takes the two words “thus” as referring to the passage below about liberating all sentient beings; but then the veins and threads before and after would not run through, and moreover the text below already has its own phrase “should thus subdue their minds.” Another explanation takes the two words “thus” as referring to the passage in the section of setting forth where the World-Honored One puts on his robe and takes up his bowl, down to spreading his seat and sitting down; this too seems inexact. Here I hold that the two words “thus” refer pointedly to the two phrases above, “well protects in thought” and “well entrusts,” and carry the meaning of a present pointing, that it is exactly so right now. The passage about putting on the robe and taking up the bowl is the distant vein; the two phrases about protecting in thought and entrusting are the near vein. Since one knows the near vein, the distant vein runs through of itself. By the Dharmakaya Tathagata displaying the appearance of an ordinary man in the dust of toil, there is no self-appearance, no Dharma-appearance, and also no no-Dharma-appearance. Therefore good men and women should likewise, as I do, dwell without abiding in appearances. When ordinary beings do not abide in appearances, they abide in no-Dharma-appearance. Once one abides, one goes astray; the deluded mind arises and ceases and cannot be subdued. Therefore good men and women should, upon the Tathagata's dressing and eating, comprehend the principle of not grasping at either extreme and thus subdue it. Pitiable, afflicted sentient beings — whether rich or poor, their whole lives are spent busying themselves for food and clothing. Whatever profession they follow, it is all begging for food. To rise in the morning and hurry into the city to work is to enter the city to beg. To begin and end work on time is to have begged in order from house to house. Begging is important indeed, but when the matter is done one should return to one's original place. The fault of ordinary beings is that for the sake of food and clothing they cannot but chase outward; in the end they forget the master and no longer return to their original place. Therefore when work is done, one should quickly turn back, quiet the mind a little, and turn the light inward, not doing irrelevant things. This is the student of the Buddha's Way spreading his seat and sitting down. We can bring the words and phrases of the sutra back upon our own persons, and we will have benefit of ourselves. If one can truly, amid ordinary daily use, turn the light back at all times, that is subduing, that is not grasping at either extreme, that is cultivating in accord with the nature-substance. Then even the recitation of the Buddha's name is done well.
(N) Next, according with the purport and requesting detail.
[“Yes indeed, World-Honored One! We wish and long to hear it.”]

“Yes” is a word of assent. The sound entered the mind and penetrated it: he had already understood thoroughly the principle of thus dwelling and thus subduing. The Tathagata's protecting in thought and entrusting others could not see, but Subhuti alone could see. Requesting on behalf of the assembly about dwelling and subduing, he had indeed received the Buddha's praise. The compiler of the sutra, setting the word “indeed” after “yes,” writes out the scene of Subhuti's joy and delight in his life, rejoicing that his comprehension was without error. Yet because the assembly had not understood, he asked again. “Wish” means aspiration. “Long” means delight. “Desire” means to seek. If one only has the aspiration in the mind but no delight, one hears perhaps without earnestness. And if one can delight but does not seek, one hears perhaps without depth. These three words advance layer by layer, expressing the assembly's thirsting admiration. They may also express the thirsting admiration for the afflicted beings of the Dharma-ending age. The word “hear” corresponds to the word “hear” in “thus have I heard” at the sutra's beginning. If Subhuti had not wished and longed and desired to hear, how could Ananda have heard it?

There are three kinds of hearing. First, hearing the words: the ear-faculty produces consciousness and hears only the words. Second, hearing the meaning: the mental consciousness takes up the meaning from the words. Third, hearing the intent: the spirit is gathered and the mind unified, seeking the meaning and taking the intent. Now, hearing these words of thus dwelling and thus subduing, one will surely gain the intent, forget the meaning, and leave behind the words, dissolving them back into one's own nature. Everyone inherently possesses the unmoving such nature, yet ignorance obstructs it, so that the deluded mind arises and ceases without pause. Therefore students should exert effort on the word “hear.” To turn the hearing around and hear one's own nature, illuminating at all times and hearing at all times, is to know that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are three with no difference. Therefore if one makes the word “hear” into the work of turning the hearing around, one can dissolve it back into one's own nature.

blocks.text: The Great Vehicle's True Teaching, Part Three

inline.s: (N) Next, the detailed discourse. In two parts: (O) first, clarifying non-dwelling by way of objects, to reveal the right wisdom of prajna; next, clarifying non-dwelling by way of mind, to manifest the principle-substance of prajna. (O) First, again in two: (P) first, pointing directly to non-dwelling to generate faith; next, drawing out non-dwelling to open understanding. (P) First, again in three: (Q) first, the explicit indication; next, generating faith; third, the comparison of merit. (Q) First, again in two: (R) first, clarifying that bringing forth the mind free of appearances is itself subduing; next, clarifying that not dwelling in appearances is itself right dwelling. (R) First, again in three: (S) first, marking and showing; next, the direct clarification; third, questioning and explaining.
(S) First, marking and showing.
[The Buddha told Subhuti: “All bodhisattva-mahasattvas should thus subdue their minds.”]

The phrase “the Buddha told” was set down by the compiler of the sutra. Wherever this phrase is set, it shows that what is said here is most essential and must not be passed over lightly in reading. The phrase “all bodhisattvas” refers to the good men and good women who have brought forth the great aspiration. Whenever “bodhisattva-mahasattva” is spoken, there are two meanings. One is the great bodhisattva among bodhisattvas, as when one speaks of the bodhisattva-mahasattva Avalokiteshvara, which names a single person. The other is a general designation of many, meaning bodhisattvas, or great bodhisattvas. Those who bring forth the aspiration are not one person only, and so it says “all.” “All” means “every.” Since many are spoken of here, it is a general designation. One should know that this sutra is fundamentally the supreme vehicle, and so all who bring forth the aspiration to learn it are great bodhisattvas. Yet their faculties differ: though they alike bring forth the great aspiration, those whose bringing forth is complete and ultimate can become great bodhisattvas, while those whose bringing forth is not complete and ultimate can only become bodhisattvas. In saying this the Buddha also hoped that everyone would bring forth the aspiration completely and ultimately. What is meant by complete and ultimate? If one brings forth the mind to attain Buddhahood above and transform sentient beings below, then one is a bodhisattva. But if one knows that one brings forth the mind to attain above and transform below, and further knows that though attaining above one in truth attains nothing, and though transforming below one in truth transforms nothing — that is, attaining above without attaining and transforming below without transforming — then the nature-virtue is ultimate, essence and function are perfect, and one is a great bodhisattva. There are many such matters in the world: though what one studies is the unsurpassed great Dharma, one's accomplishment is very small indeed. All because one does not know how to cultivate according to Dharma, and because the aspiration one brings forth is too small. Take the practice of Buddha-recitation: it is fundamentally the most perfect and most sudden of unsurpassed wondrous Dharmas. Yet if one knows only to save oneself, then this Dharma of the supreme vehicle is not merely insufficient to be the Great Vehicle — it actually becomes the Small Vehicle. Therefore one can only be reborn in the lowest grade, and for many kalpas cannot open the flower and see the Buddha. This is because one contravenes the Buddha's compassionate vow and does not know how to cultivate in accord with the nature. One may even fall short of the lowest grade, and be able to be born only in the city of doubt; and one must then cultivate for a long time before one can leave the city of doubt and be born in the Land of Peace and Nurture. Does one not then fail the Buddha's kindness above and fail one's own spirit below? Why is it so? All because one does not understand the reason for the unsurpassed great Dharma. Therefore the first thing in learning the Buddha's Way is to open wisdom. To open wisdom, in its very first step, is to understand principle. If one does not understand the true principle, the aspiration one brings forth cannot reach the supreme. Understanding principle is not a matter of analyzing words and phrases only; one must cultivate contemplation. How does one cultivate contemplation? One must read the great-vehicle sutras much, and further must shut out outer conditions and gather in body and mind. If one does not first gather this mind into one place, how can one give rise to contemplation in dependence on the words? Therefore it is said that precepts give rise to concentration, and concentration gives rise to wisdom. Precepts shut out outer conditions. The word “concentration” has shallow and deep levels: when first taking up practice, one must forcibly gather the mind into one place, making it still and collected and not scattering, and only then can contemplation arise. When contemplative wisdom has arisen, the great concentration is already within it, and no forcing is needed. Therefore, as for “calming and insight”: calming comes from insight, and when insight is accomplished, calming comes of itself. Why? Because when insight is accomplished, deluded thoughts are wholly removed, and that is calming — it is not the suppression and secret attainment of a stagnant stillness. In sum, the two words “concentration” and “wisdom” give rise to each other and cannot be rigidly viewed as two separate pieces. Therefore it is said that they are like the two wheels of a cart; and it is also said that calming is the insight within calming. Calming and insight are the essential work of learning the Buddha's Way, and what has been said above is again an essential principle within calming and insight, which one must not fail to know. Why is one who has just brought forth the aspiration at once called a bodhisattva-mahasattva? Because he can bring forth the great aspiration, he has the qualifications to become a bodhisattva-mahasattva, and so he is addressed by this title. That is the first reason. The Buddha's calling him so is to make the person directly undertake it and not lose the victory himself. That is the second reason. The World-Honored One is equal, equal; he regards sentient beings as originally the same as the Buddha. If so, to call one who has brought forth the supreme aspiration a bodhisattva-mahasattva is hardly strange. That is the third reason.

“Thus” refers to the text of the direct clarification below. “Subdue their minds” means causing deluded thoughts not to arise, and also causing the unenlightened to become enlightened. Above, the question first asked how they should dwell. The Buddha's general indication also first said they should thus dwell; why, then, in the detailed discourse does he first speak of subduing? The essential meaning here should be clarified in three layers. All sentient beings have from the first been unenlightened; now, though they have brought forth the supreme mind of enlightenment, it is only the initial mind of enlightenment that has been aroused. Their unenlightened deluded habits have not been removed in the least — how could there be a true mind to dwell? If one thinks that one sees the true mind at the first arousal of enlightenment, then this very thought is still a deluded thought. Therefore for one who has just brought forth the aspiration, the only way to begin is subduing. The ancients said: “Only seek to put an end to delusion; do not go looking further for the true.” This is the meaning. One should know that our mind, though wholly unenlightened, is in fact wholly a manifestation of original enlightenment. This is what is called the harmony of true and deluded, which is named consciousness. One need only remove the deluded mind part by part, and the true mind will appear part by part. When delusion is exhausted and the mind is empty, then the initial enlightenment merges with the original enlightenment. There is from the first no need to speak of dwelling or not dwelling. This is why he does not speak of dwelling but first speaks of subduing — that is the first reason.

Not only at the first bringing forth of the aspiration should one begin from subduing; from beginning to end there is only the work of subduing, and even at Buddhahood there is nothing dwelt in. One should know that deluded thought and ignorance (ignorance is deluded thought) take destruction as their mark. In cultivation up to the stage of faith one can only suppress, not yet destroy. Entering from the ten faiths into the first dwelling, one first destroys one part of ignorance and realizes one part of Dharmakaya (that is, first sees one part of the true mind). Ten parts accomplished are but one part; how can one dwell? To be named “dwelling” makes clear that one does not retrogress from supreme, perfectly equal, perfect enlightenment. From there one advances step by step, passing through the ten dwellings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, and the four preparatory practices, and then ascends the grounds; and only at the eighth ground is one called a non-learner, and ignorance is nearly exhausted. Yet the Buddhas of the ten directions still earnestly urge one on, that one should fulfill one's original vow, broadly save sentient beings, and not dwell in nirvana. Thereupon one passes through the ninth and tenth grounds up to equal enlightenment, and there is still one last part of ignorance. (One may see that only at equal enlightenment are nine parts destroyed.) One must still destroy it with vajra wisdom before one attains ultimate enlightenment. And even then one does not dwell in birth and death, nor dwell in nirvana. Thus one may know that even at the stage of Buddhahood it is still dwelling yet not dwelling, not dwelling yet dwelling. Is not our World-Honored One's showing himself the same as an ordinary man a model of not dwelling yet dwelling? If so, then from beginning to end there is nothing dwelt in, and there is only subduing — this is clear. That is the second reason.

Although Subhuti earlier first asked about dwelling, his gaze was in fact fixed on subduing. For since dwelling could not be attained, he next asked about subduing. Otherwise, asking only “how should they dwell” would have sufficed; why add another phrase? And the general indication both said “should thus dwell” and again said “thus subdue”: the intent is the same. Here the words have an order, but the meaning is one thread throughout. Apart from subduing there is no other method of advancing in practice. That is the third reason.
(R) Next, the direct clarification.

[“All the kinds of sentient beings — those born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born from moisture, those born by transformation; those with form, those without form, those with thought, those without thought, those neither with thought nor without thought — I cause all of them to enter nirvana without residue and be liberated. And though I thus liberate immeasurable, countless, boundless sentient beings, in truth no sentient being attains liberation.”]

When the four elements and five aggregates come together through many conditions and the appearance of birth appears, this is called a sentient being. This is the original meaning of the name “sentient being.” Extended, it means that the kinds are many and numerous, and these are called sentient beings. People today know only the extended meaning and have lost the original meaning. They do not know that the original meaning is most wondrous, for it causes one to contemplate that fundamentally there is no birth, and that the very substance is empty. How is this shown? It is only the coming together of many conditions that is named “birth”; the nature-substance was never born at all, and so it is said that fundamentally there is no birth. Since fundamentally there is no birth, now there is also no ceasing. And since it is the gathering of conditions that produces the appearance of birth, when the conditions disperse it ceases at once — is this not the very substance being empty? This is spoken by way of appearance. Spoken by way of nature: the nature does not arise because of this; though the appearances of birth and ceasing are manifold, what have they to do with the substance? Therefore it is said that the very substance is empty. Exhausting all sentient beings, their number is many, and so it says “all.” Their kinds are numerous, and so it also says “the kinds of.” What are their kinds? From those born from eggs to those neither with thought nor without thought.

In the Buddhist sutras the categories of sentient beings are sometimes divided by the six paths, wishing people to understand the principle of rebirth. Sometimes they are divided by the twelve kinds of birth (as in the eighth fascicle of the Shurangama Sutra), wishing people to understand the principle of the ten habitual causes and the six retributions of interaction. Sometimes they are divided by the three realms, wishing people to understand their heights and supports, and that they do not escape the scope of form and desire. Here too the division is by the three realms, but it does not say desire realm, form realm, and formless realm, because the formless realm still has a special physiology which must be specially brought out if it is to be thorough. It is also to make people understand why sentient beings cannot escape the three realms: not only is grasping at form and grasping at desire an obstruction; there is also a fundamental obstruction which must be thoroughly understood and counteracted before one can enter nirvana without residue and be liberated.

First, the desire realm. The desire realm has two parts. First, the upper realm, which is the six heavens of desire. (The Heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, the Yama Heaven, the Tushita Heaven, the Heaven of Enjoying Transformations, and the Heaven of Freely Enjoying Others' Transformations.) Because their merit surpasses that of humans, they are born in heaven; because they still have sexual desire, they dwell in the desire realm; because their desire-thoughts are comparatively thin, they are born only by transformation, and do not have the three births from eggs, wombs, or moisture. Second, the lower realm, which is humans, animals, ghosts, and hells. (The asuras are apportioned among the heavens — by transformation — among humans — by the womb, those who fall from the heavens — among animals — by moisture, the lowest and most inferior, born in the heart of the great sea, roaming the sky by day and returning to the water at night — and among ghosts — by the egg, who by the power of protecting the Dharma ride their spiritual powers into the air. See the ninth fascicle of the Shurangama.) Hell-beings are born by transformation; ghosts are born by the womb or by transformation; humans and animals have all four kinds of birth. All of these have their very life and destiny by way of sexual desire. When guilt is heavy and passion abundant, one falls lower and lower and drops into hell. As it gradually lightens, one dwells in the human path. The heavens of the form realm and above (the form realm has eighteen heavens: the first, second, and third dhyanas have three heavens each, and the fourth dhyana has nine) are all born by transformation. (The form realm also has the Heaven of No Thought, but since it has form, it is not included in the formless realm.) Thus merely mentioning egg, womb, moisture, and transformation already includes the three realms completely. Yet because the special physiology of the form realm and above is not made evident, he further speaks of those with form and those without form. Because they have no desire, they are born by transformation in the form realm through the power of concentration: this is what differs from the desire realm. And because they can further not grasp at the appearance of a body of form, they are born by transformation in the formless realm through the power of concentration: this is what differs from the form realm. Merely mentioning with form and without form also includes the three realms completely, for below the desire realm none lacks a body of form. Yet below the heavens of desire there is not only transformation-birth; therefore he must first speak of egg, womb, moisture, and transformation for the physiology of the lower realm to be complete. Further, within the formless realm, according to the depth of the power of concentration, there is again a special physiology which cannot but be brought out and made evident. Therefore he further speaks of those with thought, those without thought, and those neither with thought nor without thought. The four heavens of the formless realm are: the Sphere of Boundless Space, the Sphere of Boundless Consciousness, the Sphere of Nothing Whatsoever, and the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception. The Sphere of Boundless Space and the Sphere of Boundless Consciousness are the “with thought” mentioned here. Because the appearance of form is already emptied, it is called the Sphere of Boundless Space. (The formless realm has only no karmic-fruit form, because those there have cut off desire and do not grasp at the appearance of a body of form. Yet it has concentration-fruit form, subtle in color, invisible to those below the form realm; hence it is called the formless realm.) When the coarse (form realm) and turbid (desire realm) body of form is already emptied, one does not cling to and begrudge consciousness within the body of form; therefore it is called the Sphere of Boundless Consciousness. “Consciousness” means the eight consciousnesses. (Spoken of the eight consciousnesses together, not referring solely to the eighth, the alaya.) The harmony of true and deluded is named consciousness. Because of consciousness there is thought; “thought” refers to the seventh consciousness's constant and deliberate weighing and clinging to a self, and to the sixth consciousness's discrimination and universal imagining. The two words “with thought” cover form and desire. No sentient being of the form or desire realms lacks consciousness. Because of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, they cling to the body of form as a self; because they cling to the body of form, they give rise to all kinds of thoughts of greedy desire. Yet below the form realm there is not only consciousness, but also form and desire as well. Therefore he must first speak of egg, womb, moisture, and transformation, and of having form, in order to make clear their difference from the formless realm. As for “without thought” and above, these are the special physiology of the formless realm, and so it must be brought out and made evident. This makes clear that it is not only by having no karmic-fruit form that they differ from the form and desire realms. This is the Heaven of Nothing Whatsoever of the formless realm: it means that the sixth consciousness's discriminating deluded thought is nothing whatsoever, because they constantly dwell in concentration; and the seventh consciousness's clinging to a self is also nothing whatsoever, because in concentration there is no deliberation, and they do not cling to the body of form of the Sphere of Boundless Consciousness. Thus their concentration is deeper than before. “Neither with thought nor without thought” is the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception of the formless realm. Here concentration is deeper still, and the eighth, the alaya, is now hidden and now apparent, yet consciousness has not been turned into wisdom. To call it “with thought” is wrong, and to call it “without thought” is also wrong. One should know that the “nothing whatsoever” spoken of before is not truly able to be nothing whatsoever; it is only that the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are temporarily suppressed, and they themselves think there is nothing. Why? When the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are turned, the eighth consciousness and the first five are turned along with them; how could they still be now hidden and now apparent? Moreover they are mistaken: the eighth consciousness is originally a manifestation of the true mind; how can it be nothing whatsoever, and why need it be nothing whatsoever? One need only turn it. When the sixth consciousness is turned, it becomes the wisdom of wondrous observation; when the seventh is turned, it becomes the wisdom of equality; the eighth is then turned along with them and becomes the great perfect mirror wisdom, and the first five are likewise turned and become the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done. Only then are essence and function fully revealed; how then could they be nothing? It is all because they do not know the Buddha's principle and rely wholly on secret attainment without skillful means. Therefore, even though the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception has a long life of eighty thousand kalpas, one still falls in the end.

All outsiders do not know the nature; the Confucians are likewise. “What Heaven has mandated is called the nature” — but the nature is not mandated by Heaven. Some say that “mandated by Heaven” means that it is so of itself by principle; this goes against Confucius's meaning. The Book of Changes says: “That which establishes the Way of Heaven is called yin and yang.” It also says: “The alternation of one yin and one yang is called the Way; that which continues it is good, and that which completes it is the nature.” This is the origin of taking what Heaven mandates as the nature. What is meant by “so of itself by principle”? Mencius said: “Food and sex are the nature.” How could food and sex be within the nature? It is only that the seeds of habitual tendencies from beginningless kalpas make it so. This is precisely mistaking the discriminating mind for the nature. As for the Song Confucians Zhou, Cheng, Zhang, and Zhu, they plagiarized the surface phrases of the Chan gate (not even amounting to a hair of the skin) and discoursed grandly on the nature and principle. Neither Buddhist nor Confucian, they misled the Dharma and misled people; nothing could be worse than this. For all who first take in their words, the Buddha's principle can never be understood, and the truth of Confucius is likewise obstructed and does not appear. One should know that Confucius, as to what lies beyond the six directions, preserved it and did not discuss it, and so he spoke only of what Heaven mandates from above. Though this is not thorough, it can cause people to revere Heaven's mandate and stand in awe of Heaven's majesty, and so to establish the utmost of the human way. Therefore Confucius was truly a great sage of the world, to be admired and revered. Mencius and Xunzi both failed to fathom him deeply. The Han Confucians attended exclusively to glosses and exegesis and were blind to the great meaning; yet this still had its merit. Had it not been for the Han Confucians' labor of collation and collection, how could later people have understood the classics and their glosses, or how could they have seen them? The Song men, by contrast, created a style of their own and thought themselves directly in receipt of the mind-seal, unaware that the learning of Confucius was thereby obscured — their guilt is great. The abolition of Confucius in the revolution was in truth a mistaking of Song learning for Confucian learning; how much more than the guilt of slandering the Buddha-Dharma is that? How lamentable.

As for egg, womb, moisture, and transformation: egg is spoken of first because the egg includes womb, moisture, and transformation. It dwells in the mother's womb and is nourished by blood, which is moisture; what was not and now is, is transformation. The womb does not include the egg but does include moisture and transformation, and so it is spoken of next. Moisture includes transformation but not egg or womb, and so comes next. (Those born from moisture are born by transformation upon damp ground, receiving the qi of yin and yang. Because they must be on damp ground, it is called birth from moisture.) Transformation-birth arises suddenly from nothing and does not include egg, womb, or moisture, and so comes next again. This is spoken by way of the complexity and simplicity of birth. Further, egg, womb, moisture, and transformation are placed first because they include desire, form, and consciousness. “With form” does not include desire but does include consciousness, and so comes next. “Without form” does not include form or desire but does have consciousness, and so comes next again. “With form” and “without form” are spoken by way of the coarseness and subtlety of form-appearance. “With thought” makes clear that although they have no form, thought of consciousness still arises, and so comes next again. “Without thought” makes clear that the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are already suppressed and thought too is absent, and so it comes next in order. “Neither with thought nor without thought” makes clear that not only are the sixth and seventh consciousnesses absent, but the eighth is also half suppressed, and so it is placed last. This is spoken by way of the rise and fall of passion and consciousness. For each earlier one necessarily includes the later, while each later one does not include the earlier. As for egg, womb, moisture, and transformation, though one cannot wholly judge them as superior or inferior by their order, yet taking desire, form, and consciousness together, the earlier are inferior to the later, and the later surpass the earlier.

That the Buddha classified in such detail without shrinking from prolixity is no idle passage. The intent is to make one know that though the kinds of sentient beings are many, they do not escape the three matters of consciousness, form, and desire, and that it is herein that they become sentient beings. Now, having brought forth the supreme mind of enlightenment and wishing to cause all sentient beings to attain supreme enlightenment, one cannot do so without cutting off sexual desire, not grasping at form-appearance, and turning consciousness into wisdom. When delusion is exhausted and the mind is empty, and the karmic consciousness is turned, then the mind of birth and cessation ceases, one emerges from the sea of birth and death, and realizes and enters the perfect and luminous nature-sea that is neither born nor ceasing. This is what is meant by entering nirvana without residue, and this is what is meant by liberation. The Mahayana nirvana has two kinds. (1) With residue: the branch and tip ignorance (that is, the delusions of view and thought) has already been cut off, but the root ignorance (that is, the karmic consciousness, which is the very first unenlightened stirring; also called the ignorance of the mark of birth, and also called fundamental ignorance) remains uncut. Hence it is called “with residue.” (2) Without residue: the karmic consciousness is wholly emptied (that is, consciousness is turned into wisdom), and no remainder of ignorance is left. (This differs from the Small Vehicle's “with residue” and “without residue.” There it means that what was to be learned is done, and there remains a body of suffering retribution not yet exhausted: this is called nirvana with residual dependence — the so-called emergence from the affliction-obstruction while still having a body of suffering as dependence. When this retribution-body is exhausted, it is called nirvana without residual dependence — the so-called ashes of the body and extinction of wisdom.) Nirvana without residue is the name for the fruit of ultimate enlightenment, because equal enlightenment still has one last part of ignorance not yet exhausted. (That is, the subtle karmic consciousness, the so-called ignorance of the mark of birth.)

Nirvana in Sanskrit is fully said parinirvana; it means not born and not ceasing, and refers to the nature-substance. It is also translated as “liberation” and as “non-doing.” (From this one may see that the Buddhist canon borrows a pre-existing name and that its meaning differs utterly from the Confucian and Daoist schools; indeed those two schools differ greatly from each other as well. Laozi's non-doing means to guide according to circumstance, not seeking brilliant achievements or a brilliant name. Because it never manifests any trace of doing, it is called non-doing, also called purity and stillness. From Cao Shen's mistaking purity and stillness for doing nothing, it came to be criticized by the Confucians. In Cao Shen's time it was proper to rest and recuperate, and so even the misunderstanding was beneficial. The pure conversation of the Jin, by contrast, greatly harmed the state. How severe are the calamities that come from not understanding the true meaning! Confucius's non-doing, on the other hand, describes Yao and Shun: knowing the worthy and employing them well, folding the hands and letting the robes hang down while governing, and the meaning of “vast, so that the people could find no name for it.”) “Enter” means to realize and enter, that is, to cause sentient beings to realize and enter the fruit of ultimate enlightenment. “Liberate” is the so-called “when birth and cessation have ceased, still extinction appears before one.” “Ferry across” means to ferry across the two kinds of birth and death, the fragmentary and the transformational. That the Sanskrit sound is not given here but its meaning is spoken instead has two reasons. First, to make clear that what is called entering nirvana without residue is nothing other than this: extinguishing the mind of birth and cessation of consciousness, form, and desire, one ferries across the sea of birth and death and reaches the other shore of nirvana. Second, for convenience of wording: below it says “liberated immeasurable, countless, boundless sentient beings,” and if “liberated” were replaced by “nirvana,” it would not be easy to understand. This is the skill of the translator. Nirvana without residue is translated by the Dharma-character school as “nirvana of no abode,” making clear that one neither dwells in birth and death nor dwells in nirvana. This translation and Kumarajiva's each have their own purport, and both are excellent. As for calling a cultivator's passing “nirvana” or “entering extinction,” this is a borrowing to make clear that he does not abide in appearances but enters stillness. People of the world mostly misunderstand nirvana and entering extinction as a special name for death, and the Song Confucians further mistake still extinction for doing nothing at all. How far off they are.

The Dharma-character school says that three and a half kinds of sentient beings cannot become Buddhas: the fixed-nature arhat, the fixed-nature bodhisattva, and the icchantika (one without roots of faith) — these are the three; and the indefinite-nature is added as the half. How is it, then, that here all are caused to become Buddhas? One should know that the sutra says: “The Buddha-seed arises from conditions.” It also says (Nirvana Sutra): “Whoever has a mind shall certainly become a Buddha.” And it also says (Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment): “Those with the nature and those without the nature alike accomplish the Buddha's Way.” How is this attained? The Buddha-nature, though inherently possessed by sentient beings, yet the Buddha-seed must await conditions to arise. What the Dharma-character school says of “cannot accomplish” means that without the seed one certainly cannot accomplish; it does not mean that the fixed-nature and the icchantika have no Buddha-nature. Therefore the two words “seed” and “nature” must not be confused. Students of the nature school often cling to the nature and are blind to the seed, as when they cling to the nature and discard practice. Students of the character school, in turn, often cling to the seed and are blind to the nature. Both are at fault for not understanding the purport of the sutras.

“Thus” refers to the sentence above about causing them to enter nirvana without residue. “Immeasurable” means that the kinds are not limited in measure: whatever their faculties, superior or inferior, all are liberated. “Countless” means that the many and the few are not counted. Yet one might liberate only one world, or one world for one kalpa or ten kalpas, and that too could be called immeasurable and countless. But here it is not so: it is boundless. “Boundless” means extending horizontally through the ten directions and vertically to the end of the three periods. Therefore “boundless” is the general term, and “immeasurable” and “countless” the particular. Because the liberation is boundless, it can be immeasurable and countless. “In truth no sentient being attains liberation”: this contemplates the principle that there is no birth and no attainment, and it is truly nothing, not imaginatively nothing. The ancient worthies made a contemplation of it in five meanings, most wondrously. (1) Condition-born: all sentient beings are nothing but the false combination of the four elements and five aggregates; the very substance is empty — how could there be sentient beings? (2) Same substance: I and sentient beings differ in appearance but are in truth the same in nature; this is what is called the one Dharma-realm. If so, then to see sentient beings is for one's own mind to take hold of one's own mind, and the non-illusory becomes illusory Dharmas. (3) Fundamentally still: what is called a sentient being is the appearance of birth falsely produced by the union of conditions; its nature is fundamentally unborn. Being fundamentally unborn, it is fundamentally unceasing — how could there be any so-called attaining of nirvana? (4) No thought: contemplating by the three meanings above, one may know that to see sentient beings and to see sentient beings attaining nirvana is wholly deluded thought and discrimination. If there is no thought, then sentient beings are not, and attainment also is not. (5) Equal: as said above, one may see that all sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas, equal, equal. Therefore it is said: “Equal is the true Dharma-realm; the Buddha does not liberate sentient beings.” If one sees sentient beings attaining liberation, one contravenes the equal Dharma-realm. In sum, the nature is true and appearances are illusory. If one would accomplish supreme enlightenment, one should realize the true nature. Then in all circumstances one should not grasp at appearances but return to the nature; returning to the nature is what is true. Therefore, spoken by way of the nature, the liberation of sentient beings is truly nothing, not imaginatively nothing — this is clear.

Someone asks: the passage above says “should thus subdue their minds,” and the two words “thus” refer precisely to this section. Yet on reading it one truly does not understand what is meant by subduing — what is being subdued? Is merely bringing forth the vast mind free of appearances enough to subdue? The answer: this meaning is most refined, and should be analyzed for you.

What is called subduing is subduing the deluded mind. The deluded mind is the discriminating mind. Discrimination arises from clinging to a self, and so the view of self is the root of discrimination. Here, therefore, it is removed at the root: when the view of self is removed, discriminating deluded thought is transformed of itself. Further, this section's text lays its weight on the last sentence; all that precedes is to bring about this sentence. Because he wishes to say that in truth no sentient being attains liberation, he first speaks of liberating boundless sentient beings into nirvana without residue. Because he wishes to speak of causing them to enter nirvana without residue, he first speaks of the kinds of sentient beings as no more than consciousness, form, and desire. If so, then knowing how sentient beings come to be, one knows how to liberate sentient beings. Knowing that boundless sentient beings are nothing but illusory appearances conjured by consciousness, form, and desire, one knows to extinguish the appearance of birth and cessation of consciousness, form, and desire and cause them to enter the unborn and unceasing; and then in truth there are no sentient beings, and in truth no sentient being attains liberation. Why? Sentient beings are obstructed only by consciousness, form, and desire; their original nature is from the first unborn and unceasing, and moreover is of one substance with me — what is called a sentient being, and what is called attainment? When this contemplation becomes ripe, the clinging to a self-view is transformed without one's being aware of it. Why? Because one knows that I too am a sentient being; because one knows that the very substance is empty; because one knows that when thought arises it exists, and that if there is no thought in it, all is non-existent; because one knows that fundamentally it is equal. This is why the Great Vehicle Dharma is skillful: it is subduing without subduing.

There is an especially essential meaning here that should be further explained. (1) Deluded thought has deep roots; one has just aroused enlightenment and one's power of the Way is slight — how can one oppose it? Moreover, true mind and deluded mind are originally of one substance. When a thought stirs, the whole true becomes deluded; when the mind opens and thought ceases, the whole deluded is precisely the true. Why then must one remove it? For these two reasons, what is called removing delusion is only provisionally named removal; there is in truth nothing to remove. What is called subduing is a skillful shifting, causing it to return and submit; it does not mean opposing and destroying it. Now, causing one to bring forth the mind free of appearances is precisely a skillful means of making it great and transforming it. (2) Why is it that bringing forth the great mind can transform it? One should know that ordinary beings have narrow minds, and therefore cling to a self; the more they cling, the narrower they become. If one brings forth the mind of vast liberation of the boundless and contemplates it purely for a long time, without knowing it the clinging is dissolved. (3) Ordinary beings know only that there is a self. If one were told to contemplate no-self upon one's own person, one would certainly be unable to enter. Now one is told to look from the opposite side, toward the broad and wide, and contemplate that there are no sentient beings; then, the mind being already expanded, in a single confronting glance one sees clearly and easily that this self of mine is likewise condition-born and fundamentally still. All of these are skillful gates of making great and transforming. (4) The root of the delusions of view and thought is the view of self. Now by the method of shifting and silently transforming, it is cut off without one's being aware — truly the hardest and sharpest vajra. (5) The clinging to self is the manas consciousness. With a self, there are the discriminations of person, sentient being, and lifespan. Discrimination is the sixth consciousness. Now, not grasping at anything is turning the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. When the sixth and seventh are turned, the first five and the eighth are turned along with them and become wisdom. This is what is called prajna-paramita. (6) To liberate all sentient beings into Buddhahood negates emptiness; that in truth no sentient being is liberated negates existence: this is the double negation. Though liberating broadly yet in truth nothing, and though in truth nothing yet liberating broadly: this is the double illumination. Contemplating negation and illumination as simultaneous as the cause, one attains the fruit of stillness and illumination as simultaneous. (7) Bringing forth the mind of broad liberation is great compassion. Contemplating that in truth there is no attainment is great wisdom. Being complete in compassion and wisdom is again the cause of not dwelling in birth and death and not dwelling in nirvana. (8) Spoken from the side of great compassion as described above, it is the cultivation of merit. Spoken from the side of great wisdom, it is the cultivation of wisdom. Cultivating both merit and wisdom is again the cause of accomplishing the doubly-endowed Honored One. One may know that all the great-vehicle Dharmas are contained herein, and that all of them are Dharmas leading straight to the jewel-land. Therefore this sutra says: “All Buddhas and all the Buddhas' Dharmas of supreme, perfectly equal, perfect enlightenment come forth from this sutra.” (9) Before being able to liberate oneself, one wishes first to liberate others: this is the bodhisattva's bringing forth of the aspiration, what is called great compassion. Now, seeing the meaning of this section, one first knows that liberating others is liberating oneself. Then within great compassion there is great wisdom — truly skillful. (10) This section causes one to bring forth vows. Students have always suffered because the great vow could not be brought forth; they may contemplate according to what was said above in (1) through (9), and the great vow complete in compassion and wisdom will arise of itself.

Further, the subduing spoken of in the section above also contains another meaning: it is to make one who brings forth the great vow firmly establish his resolve and not give rise to cowardice. This itself is subduing the mind.

In these two sections, the marking-and-showing and the direct clarification, the point is precisely to show us where the work of cultivation lies. It is most intimate and most essential. Briefly, the essential meanings are eight.

(1) Subhuti first asked about dwelling and then about subduing; the answer, however, speaks of subduing first and dwelling after. And in the answer about dwelling, it further says they should dwell nowhere. One may see that our effort is only to remove delusion. Why? The true mind does not appear wholly because of the obstruction of delusion. If delusion is not wholly removed and yet one says one peacefully dwells in the such true, then this very thought is still a deluded thought. Moreover, the Buddha, having attained ultimate realization, does not dwell in nirvana either; how then, while cultivating the cause, can one speak of dwelling? The Shurangama says: “When the knowing of enlightenment is set up, the object of illumination is produced; once the object is established, the nature of illumination perishes.” It also says: “To set up knowing upon knowing and seeing is the root of ignorance.” Thus one knows that where there is dwelling there is an object, and where there is an object there is a setting up. Where there is an object and a setting up, this is the great perfect mirror itself stained with dust, and how can its light shine everywhere? Therefore it says: “the root of ignorance, the nature of illumination perishes.” Therefore the Chan patriarchs say: “Only seek to put an end to delusion; do not go looking further for the true.” The ancient worthies also say: “Only exhaust the ordinary feelings; there is no other sagely understanding.” This says that exhausting the ordinary feelings is itself the sagely understanding. The sutra also says: “If the mad mind does not rest, when it rests, that is bodhi.” All of these explain the principle that in practice one need only subdue the deluded mind. From this one may realize that sweeping away discriminating knowledge and views is a work from first to last, and not merely the method of beginning.

(2) Subduing requires a skillful means. Without a skillful means, the deluded mind blazes up the more. Here subduing is lodged within the bringing forth of the vast mind. In other words, bringing forth the vast mind is itself subduing. If so, then subduing means making great and transforming; there is no so-called subduing, and yet it is naturally subdued. The skillful means is supreme.

(3) Subduing means subduing the deluded mind. One should know that the deluded mind is born of discrimination. The root of discrimination lies in clinging to a self. Therefore here the vast mind is used to subdue the four appearances of self, person, and the rest, and to liberate all immeasurable, countless, boundless sentient beings. With such great compassion and great pity, the two poisons of greed and anger are removed. Further, though liberating sentient beings, in truth there is nothing liberated: this is the view of non-permanence (that is, not grasping at existence). Though there is nothing liberated, yet the liberating does not cease: this is the view of non-annihilation (that is, not grasping at emptiness). Neither permanent nor annihilated, possessing this wondrous wisdom, the poison of delusion too is removed. For all ordinary beings whose view of self is heavy and whose three poisons are deep, the root of the illness is in truth the narrowness of the mind. One must use the vast mind to cure the root of the illness; solving it at the root, all the illnesses are naturally easy to remove.

(4) All sentient beings, from beginningless time until now, have never been enlightened. What is called unenlightened means not knowing that the discrimination of person and self both come from grasping at appearances. Departing from appearances and merging with the nature, all is fundamentally of one substance: how could there be difference? Because of not knowing, one clings to appearances, and the more one clings the more deluded one becomes; delusion is itself delusion. From this one establishes the mine in dependence on the self. Greed and anger contend and arise, and karma is made without end. Further, one does not understand that what is called “mine” is nothing but illusory existence born of conditions. Whether Dharma (existence) or no-Dharma (emptiness), as soon as there is any grasping, there is no understanding. The appearances of Dharma and no-Dharma both arise from the nature; and if one melts them with the nature, appearances are fundamentally no-appearance. What “mine” is there, and what self or person? Because one does not understand, one is bound by karma and has no way to be freed. Now, with the vast mind, liberating sentient beings and not grasping: this is to cause them to depart from all Dharma and no-Dharma appearances (that is, to depart from the two extremes of emptiness and existence) and to merge into the nature of one substance. If one merges into the nature, how could there still be the differing appearances of self and person? Is this not liberating oneself in liberating others? What skill could surpass this?

(5) That ordinary beings are easily turned by circumstances (circumstances being “mine”) is for no other reason than that they cling to circumstances. Even when one brings forth the aspiration and cultivates, one is not without circumstances as objects. For instance, liberating sentient beings is itself the circumstance before the mind of one who practices the great mind. Since one cannot be without circumstances as objects (without circumstances, one grasps at emptiness, and there is no way to begin cultivation), and yet one must not grasp at circumstances (grasping at circumstances is grasping at existence), here he first takes liberating yet in truth nothing liberated, causing one not to grasp at either extreme, to merge into the Middle Way, and to accord with the nature-substance. How intimate is this pointing out of the very means of entry.

(6) Here, though subduing is spoken of and dwelling is not, the meaning of dwelling is in fact silently lodged within it. That one who brings forth the great mind should first liberate sentient beings — is this not plainly showing the method of pacifying the mind? And that liberating is nothing liberated also shows that one should dwell yet dwell nowhere. This is why Maitreya's verse says “benefiting the profound mind's dwelling.” In plain terms, it is to cause one to dwell in the right wisdom of prajna: the so-called contemplative prajna, which contemplates emptiness and the provisional, not departing from the Middle Way's ultimate meaning in which emptiness and the provisional are simultaneous. Because sentient beings inherently have the illness of grasping, he does not state it plainly, but lets those who do not abide in appearances receive it themselves.

(7) The common view holds that prajna discusses profound principle, and some even fear that it leans toward emptiness, so that those who cultivate the Pure Land dare not speak of it; and those who study prajna often cling to principle and discard practice, giving others grounds for reproach. Now observe that he first speaks of subduing: one may see that if the obstruction of deluded habits is not removed, how can the right wisdom of prajna open? And he first speaks of the matter of liberating sentient beings: one may see that forging the mind through affairs is precisely where prajna begins, and how can one discuss principle apart from affairs? Further, neither of the two extremes, emptiness and existence, may be grasped at — how then could it lean toward emptiness? In such places one must pay careful attention and examine them.

(8) Here, subduing the discriminating mind is turning the sixth consciousness; and subduing the appearance of self is turning the seventh consciousness. One should know that sentient beings have from beginningless time been unenlightened, so that the pure mind of the nature does not appear but manifests as consciousness. Of the functions of consciousness, the greatest are the sixth and seventh, and so one should begin here. At this point the whole of it is consciousness — how could there be a true mind to dwell in? This is why he speaks only of subduing and not of dwelling. What is called the right wisdom of contemplative prajna is likewise still consciousness. One should know that consciousness as a thing is originally a manifestation of the nature. Used to discriminate and cling to a self, it becomes consciousness, and is named deluded. Used to subdue the discriminating clinging to self, it is a leading back to the right path, and is therefore named right wisdom. This is to use one's own spear against one's own shield, or as the saying goes, “to untie the bell one must rely on the one who tied it.” What the Chan school calls “investigating apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness” is of one flavor with this. Because one has not departed from them, it teaches departure. One should know that the thought that can depart is also consciousness. For unless one begins here, there is simply no way. And that the Chan school does not plainly say it is consciousness has the same intent as not speaking of dwelling here: this is what is meant by “of one flavor.” The Chan school sometimes on this account looks down on other Dharma-gates, saying that in the Chan school one has already departed from mind, intellect, and consciousness at the very outset. Is this not having eaten the wonder drug without knowing why the drug is wonder-working? The practice of Buddha-recitation is the same. As soon as one speaks of reciting, it is mind and consciousness. Yet one does not realize that single-minded right mindfulness is precisely what subdues the profusion of deluded thoughts. Someone may say: because it cannot depart from thought, it is in the end inferior to the Chan school's direct pointing. But one does not realize that pure mindfulness and deluded mindfulness are greatly different: deluded thoughts, the more one thinks them, the more they arise; pure mindfulness can be thought and thought until it reaches no-thought. For instance, stirring water with mud makes it the more turbid; stirring water with alum makes it clear. If one speaks of direct pointing upward, then compared with the Chan school's direct pointing upward, this is even more secure and more skillful. It is truly “fall down where you are, get up where you are” — is it not direct and to the point? Therefore in the Pure Land gate one begins precisely by turning consciousness into wisdom, precisely by subduing, precisely by the right wisdom of contemplative prajna, precisely by being mindful yet free of thought and not grasping at either extreme. Moreover, one who recites the Buddha's name should bring forth the great aspiration, universally vowing that all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm be born together in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is to use this right mindfulness to silently permeate the Dharma-realm and broadly liberate sentient beings. Is this not the same as what is said here? If one can fuse and understand this point of principle, how could one not redouble one's recitation? How could one still fear that the recitation lacks power? This is important, important.
(R) Third, questioning and explaining.
[“Why is this? Subhuti, if a bodhisattva has the appearance of a self, the appearance of a person, the appearance of a sentient being, or the appearance of a lifespan, then he is not a bodhisattva.”]
“Questioning” means raising up: raising the meaning spoken above and explaining it clearly, which is called questioning and explaining. It is the meaning of asking and answering oneself.

Person, sentient being, and lifespan are all unfolded from the self. When there is the appearance of a self, there is the opposed appearance of a person. When persons are more than one, there is the appearance of a sentient being. When the clinging view of self continues without interruption, that is the appearance of a lifespan. The four appearances are no more than one appearance of self. That he now unfolds and speaks of them is to make clear that one who clings to a self has a discriminating mind. It makes one know that the sixth consciousness is born of the manas; where there is manas, there is the sixth consciousness, and they are not apart. Such clinging to self and discrimination is the common illness of ordinary beings — how could such a one be a bodhisattva? Therefore it says “then he is not.” Thus the admonition to those who bring forth the great aspiration is most deep and earnest.

The appearance of self is born of the view of self, and the view of self is revealed by the appearance of self. The one is outward, the other inward, and from the first they are never apart. To break the appearance of self is to break the view of self. Appearances have coarse and fine: the coarse grasps at circumstances, the fine grasps at the mind. The later Zhou also said that the appearance of self is spoken by way of the mind, that is, by way of consciousness. For the eight consciousnesses are appearances manifested by the true-such mind; therefore the Consciousness-Only school is also called the Character school.

This section originally explains why the section above causes one to bring forth the great vow. Why does it not say: “Why is this? Because it is made great and transformed; because delusion is cut off; because consciousness is turned; and even because to liberate oneself one must first liberate others, and liberating others is liberating oneself”? Would this not make the meaning of the section above clearer? Why must he speak from the reverse side? Because cutting off delusion and turning consciousness and the rest are all Dharmas, and all are not to be grasped. To grasp them is again to form the appearance of self and again to form discrimination. Therefore he does not use positive formulation but negative formulation, sweeping them all away together. This is the World-Honored One's subtle intent, and also the orthodox teaching of prajna.

The four appearances are one appearance of self. When there is a self, there is the opposed appearance of a person. When those opposed are more than one, that is the appearance of a sentient being. When the appearance of self in the deluded mind continues thought after thought without forgetting, that is the appearance of a lifespan. If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings being liberated and thinks, “I liberate them,” then he has the appearance of self, and all four appearances arise together. When there are four appearances, there is a discriminating mind. To have a discriminating mind is to be an ordinary being, not a bodhisattva. The cultivator should first of all set aside the word “I” and bring forth the aspiration for the sake of all sentient beings: this is subduing the appearance of self. “I cause all of them to enter nirvana without residue and be liberated” — sentient beings are stiff and strong, and to make them cultivate is already not easy, how much more to end birth and death! Yet he asks nothing of them: whether human or non-human, he liberates them all into Buddhahood, and they are fundamentally already Buddhas. This is subduing the appearance of a person. “Liberating immeasurable, countless, boundless sentient beings,” yet in the mind not giving rise to the thought of how they can all be liberated: this is subduing the appearance of a lifespan. “In truth no sentient being attains liberation”: this is subduing the appearance of a sentient being. Why must one thus subdue? Because one who brings forth the supreme aspiration must practice the bodhisattva's practices, the practices of Universal Good. If he has the four appearances, how can he be called a bodhisattva?

The Buddha would have cultivators give rise to contemplation from the words. Without the work of contemplation, the ordinary feelings cannot be turned; therefore students must begin here. Now, from this passage of the sutra text, I will set out in detail the method of contemplation. The ancients for the most part did not explain contemplation in detail. Contemplation is observation. (It was originally translated as “thinking,” which is pondering in the mind.) The Chan school holds that one may not investigate with mind, intellect, and consciousness, which plainly teaches people not to use thought. Yet it also says one must not fall into the armor of no-thought, which again means one must use thought. The reason for this is that ordinary beings have many views of knowing, and so one must go straight in single-file, first cutting away the branches and leaves. In the Chan school, when looking at a meditation topic, one must give rise to doubt. If one does not think, from where does the doubt arise? Contemplation is pondering. Yet pondering alone will not do, and so one also uses “illumination.” Illumination is the Chan school's “looking.” If one gives rise to contemplation from the words, then as soon as one leaves the words and returns to the mind, one can illuminate and abide. When illuminating and abiding, if one says there is pondering, there is yet no pondering; if one says there is no pondering, it is yet not no-pondering. At this time wisdom naturally opens in the mind. What is opening? It is deluded thought stopping and abiding in original enlightenment.

Prajna has the prajna of words, the prajna of contemplation, and the prajna of true suchness. “Words” refers to the text of the sutra. “True suchness” refers to the nature that everyone inherently possesses. The Buddha teaches prajna in the hope that students will realize this inherently possessed nature. How can one realize it? One should give rise to contemplation from the words. If one does not contemplate, the words remain words and cannot be dissolved back into one's own nature, and no benefit is gained. We read and recite the Diamond Sutra precisely in the hope of dissolving it back into our own nature; the Buddha taught this sutra for this too. If so, then the principle of contemplation and the method of contemplation cannot be unknown. Not only must prajna be contemplated; all Buddha-Dharmas, when it comes to cultivation, in a thousand myriad gates, are none of them outside contemplation. The three conditions of learning the Buddha's Way are called precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Without precepts, the three karmas of body, speech, and mind cannot be purified; therefore precepts are the foundation of study and are independent. The two words concentration and wisdom give rise to each other. Spoken of as fruit, they are concentration and wisdom; spoken of as cause, they are calming and insight. Calming is the stilling of deluded thoughts; insight is the contemplation of the true mind. Because of calming, concentration is born; because of insight, wisdom is born. This is to speak of them distributively. In fact, in the work of calming and insight there is only the one word “insight”; the two are one matter. As for calming: when first beginning, one must gather the mind into one place, which is what the ancients called concentration. In fact, a beginner does not deserve the name of concentration, yet concentration is born from it; after a long time, wisdom is born of concentration. Why? When one gate of contemplation is accomplished, wisdom arises and deluded thoughts fall away. Therefore only with wisdom can this concentration be accomplished. Moreover, when first beginning and gathering the mind into one place, one must apply great intention before it can be gathered, which shows that contemplation is present within it. So, whichever way one puts it, there is only the one word “insight.” This is why prajna does not speak of calming but of contemplation.

Contemplation has many methods; without a method one cannot give rise to contemplation. The methods differ among the schools, but their aim is one. Such are the Tiantai school's three contemplations of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; the Avatamsaka school's four unobstructed contemplations and its contemplation of the Dharma-realm; the Dharma-character school's fivefold consciousness-only contemplation; the Esoteric school's contemplation of the mandala and the contemplation of the letter A; the Chan school's looking at a meditation topic; and the Pure Land school's contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. Some say that reciting the Buddha's name is not contemplation. This is not so. One should know that reciting is contemplating. If deluded thoughts are scattered and one recites with a scattered mind, no benefit is gained. One must recite the Buddha's name with the mouth and think of Amitabha in the mind, as though he were before one's eyes. Reciting in this way, deluded thoughts have no way to arise, and this is contemplation. Therefore in applying effort nothing is more essential than cultivating contemplation. Cultivating contemplation is gathering in the faculty of mind. When the mind-faculty is gathered, the two karmas of body and speech are gathered in as well. Therefore in the Pure Land school one thinks of the Buddha in the mind, recites with the mouth, and holds the beads in the hand; in the Esoteric school one forms the contemplation in the mind, recites the mantra with the mouth, and forms the mudra with the hand. One may see that however one applies effort, one cannot do so without contemplation. The three contemplations of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, and the four unobstructed contemplations of the teaching schools, may seem to differ in method, yet their principle is one, and this must not be unknown; otherwise one cannot fuse the scriptures of the various schools, and will find contradictions.
